Higher Education’.

Resource Development was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 22
nd May, 2006. After

seeking further clarifications on it.  Accordingly, a meeting was held on the 19 th February, 2007 with the Secretary and
other representatives of the Department of Higher Education in which clarifications on certain points were sought.
Subsequently, a questionnaire was also forwarded to the Department and replies were obtained from them.

CHAPTER - I
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY GOVERNMENT
 
3.7       Major Constraints
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.7.1    Several social, economic administrative and other reasons seem to act together as constraints to access and equity
in higher education.  Factors like rural-urban divide, gender disparity, regional imbalances, decreasing public allocation,
economic hardship, increasing cost due to commercialization, etc. are some of the major reasons of this phenomena. This
scenario of higher education, particularly in the ever-expanding competitive environment, does not inspire required
confidence, if India were to play its assigned role at the global level.   The Committee, therefore, believes that India has
to rise to the occasion urgently and make its higher education system not only competitive but also accessible and
affordable to everyone.
 
Action taken
 
Observations of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted. While it is true that public allocation has been decreasing in

196thReport of Human Resource Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/196threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:42:40]
real terms over the period 1990-91 to 2002-03, Central Governments outlays in higher and technical education was more
than doubled during the last two years over the allocation for 2003-04. Higher education can be made affordable only
through a major expansion of the public system along side effective statutory regulation of fee where required. The
Constitution (93rd Amendment) Act, 2005 enables the Centre as well as States to do so.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.7.2    Dimension of this problem is not only confined to access to higher education of the age group of 18-23 years.  It
also extends to those in the need of continuous learning and are older than the age group of 18-23 years.  The Committee
feels that the demand for higher education from diverse kind of learners calls for the courses that are flexible; can be
studied off-campuses and credits received are portable.   The Committee desires the Government to take proactive
measures in this regard urgently.
 
Action taken
 
Deemed to be universities are being allowed to have off-campuses provided they maintain the requisite standards.  The
UGC has already issued guidelines for credit-based system, which is flexible and allows credit transfer. However, this
system needs to be adopted by all universities of the country and would take time, considering the autonomous decision
making processes in each University. In order to provide continuous and life long learning, the ODL System is being
strengthened. The role of the Distance Education Council is under review for making it more effective to maintain
standards of Distance Learning. Virtual Web-based learning opportunities as well as certification processes are under
development.
 
3.8       Other Imbalances
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.8.1    The Committee is dismayed to note that there was tremendous imbalance in access to higher education in urban
and rural areas.  Most of the colleges and universities, the Committee notes, are located in urban or semi-urban areas. 
Whatever colleges were in rural areas, less said is, better about their quality and output.  While only 16 out of every 1000
were college graduates in rural areas, 111 out of every 1000 belonged to this category in urban areas.  The same trend is
also discernable in relation to house-hold economic status both in rural as well as urban areas.  Higher education in the
country, the Committee notes, is thus largely a pro-rich and urban phenomenon.
 
3.8.2    Similarly, the gender disparity in higher education in India was yet another area of concern, which has been dealt
with in detail elsewhere in this Report.  The Committee is of the considered opinion that urban bias and gender disparity
in higher education are the two main stumbling blocks to access and equity in this area.  Large sections of our
population, therefore, are denied access to learning for economic, cultural, religious, geographical and other reasons.
 
Action taken (3.8.1 and 3.8.2)
 
For expanding the rural higher education base, the University Grants Commission provides assistance to Colleges and
Universities in rural and backward areas.  Even so, the Hon’ble Committee’s observation regarding the urban-rural gap
is noteworthy and shall be taken into consideration while formulating the XIth Plan with appropriate physical targets to
minimize urban bias.  Similarly steps have been taken to address gender bias. An Empowered Standing Committee of the
UGC on Women’s Studies has been entrusted the task of in-depth study of this problem and to suggest remedial
measures.  The interim reports of the said Empowered Committee are being taken into consideration in the XIth Plan
proposals.
 
3.9       Regional Disparity
 
Recommendations/Observations
3.9.4    The Committee also emphasizes the special focus for improving access and equity in remote regions and

geographically disadvantaged places. It also desires special funding and region-specific norms for North-East Region &
Jammu & Kashmir.  The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Government for setting up Central Universities in
North-Eastern States.  The Committee recommends that such universities may be set up in the remaining States of
North-Eastern region including Sikkim at the earliest. The colleges in these areas should be given special funding in
addition to normal development grants by the UGC.  The Committee desires special funding and region-specific norms
for North-East Region & Jammu & Kashmir.
 
Action taken
 
Three Central Universities have been approved “in principle” (Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh and Tripura) and Bills in this
regard have since been introduced in Parliament. Several steps have been taken in regard to the State of Jammu &
Kashmir as well. As a special measures, a total of 18 new colleges have been sanctioned in the State, including 2 women
only colleges. These institutions are being located by the State Govt. in the backward districts. A center for Kashmiri
Studies will be established with Central assistance, additional assistance to facilitate the setting up of 100 Bed Girls’
Hostel. (One each at Universities of Jammu and Kashmir), special assistance of Rs.1.00 crore each to two college, which
are one Hundred Years old, and sanction of an Academic Staff College at Jammu University and a Women’s Study
Centre at the Kashmir University are some of the initiatives.
 
3.13
          Open University
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.13.4  The Committee’s attention has been drawn to some inherent drawbacks present in this system of education.  Lack
of quality faculty members, non-availability of relevant study material, lack of basic facilities like good libraries, modern
labs, computer, multimedia facilities, etc. are the major issues that need immediate redressal.  Absence of an effective
and efficient information dissemination system to the students about various types of courses, examination schedules,
results, degrees etc. causes great hardship to students.  Even at the IGNOU (HQ), students have to run from pillar to post
for these things. The Committee, therefore, recommends that these aspects to be looked into urgently with a view to
provide an adequate and efficient delivery mechanism and support system in the IGNOU and other Open Universities.  
The Committee is of the considered view that to make Open Universities more attractive and relevant, efforts be made to
ensure quality of study material, timely dispatch thereof, dedicated teachers at the study centres, provision of necessary
infrastructure, use of ICT, etc.
 
Action taken
 
The recommendation of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted for appropriate action by IGNOU in future.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.13.5  The Committee finds that there is no accreditation system in IGNOU.   It is surprised to note that the work of
neither IGNOU nor any other State Open University any Correspondence Course Institutes (CCI) has ever been assessed
since they started functioning.  As a result, credibility of these institutions vis-a-vis mainstream education system is
poor.  The Committee, therefore, emphasizes the urgent need for an effective assessment and accreditation system for
these institutions so as to enhance and maintain quality of education provided through the distance mode.
 
Action taken
 
The observations of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted. The Distance Education Council is being reviewed for its
strengthening in this regard.
 
3.15     Women & Higher Education
 
Recommendations/Observations

3.15.7  The Department in its notes has mentioned the following schemes that were currently being run for the women:
Special scheme for construction of women hostels; establishment of women’s studies organize; Day Care organize in
universities, etc. The Committee notes that neither the Department nor the UGC had any concrete and targeted scheme or
programme for improving the participation of women in higher education.   Such an indifferent approach for this very
crucial aspect is almost perilous. The Committee, therefore, recommends that formulation of targeted/specific schemes
and programmes for this purpose needs to be done by the Government urgently. The Committee has learnt that a very
good scheme for supporting single girl child of a parent for higher education has been announced. The Committee
emphasizes the need for its wide publicity.  Sufficient funds should be provided for this purpose.
 
Action taken
 
The recommendations have been noted for consideration while formulating the XIth Plan.
 
4.5
              Promoting Research
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
4.5.2    Private people are not inclined to support research in universities and research being a capital-intensive activity,
their participation would help greatly. The needs of the institutions, research labs and industries are mutually common.
Therefore, there need to have greater degree of connectivity and cooperation. The Committee strongly feels that needs of
these three entities may be interlinked to make research more relevant and productive. Inability of researchers to secure
employment for themselves is also one of the reasons for such a state of affairs in this area. 
Action taken
 
Recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
4.5.5    The Committee also emphasizes the need for monitoring and evaluation of research in universities by setting up
Monitoring & Evaluation (ME) units under the supervision of a Committee of eminent professors from different
disciplines. It needs coordination with national laboratories. Number of fellowships also needs to be suitably enhanced
so that students are attracted to undertake research in newer areas.
 
Action taken
 
The UGC regularly monitors the progress of the research projects to ensure its smooth functioning and proper utilization
of grants. The recommendations for enhancement of number of fellowships has been noted. The UGC has been advised
for enhancement of the fellowship schemes operated under the UGC.
 
4.7.      Social Sciences & Humanities
 
Recommendations/observations
 
4.7.2   The process of privatization and liberalization have generated new demands, particularly in higher education. It
has led to considerable neglect of social sciences. These disciplines are such branches of knowledge which do not have
any immediate market value. Private  participation has been mainly confined to professional courses. Government
funding, therefore, remains the only source available for social sciences. What is more disturbing is that Government
funding is increasingly being diverted for professional institutions, thus leaving the social sciences in the state of utter
neglect. The Committee is of the view that utility of social sciences to our society, polity, economy, etc. cannot be
overlooked. They add value to one’s life and any study that is value-free, in fact, tends to become sterile. The
Committee, therefore, is of the considered opinion that this imbalance needs to be corrected immediately by making the
study of social sciences scientific, interesting and relevant to present situation. The government and the UGC may set up
an Expert Committee for presenting a blueprint for this purpose.

Action taken
 
Noted for being conveyed to UGC.
 
V.        QUALITY AND EXCELLENCE
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
5.1       The Committee notes that while setting up the universities, not much attention could be paid to the standards and
quality of teaching/learning processes. Besides, erosion in values, decline in the work ethics and dilution of norms have
also been notices in the Indian university system. Structure of governance in our educational institutions including
universities is not conducive to change of any kind, including that of curriculum.   Anything that does not change with
time becomes redundant soon in the fast moving world.
 
5.2       India, in fact, does not figure at all in the world ranking of top 100 universities.   Even among Asia Pacific
countries, India ranks 6
th in the list, with South Korea and Israel ahead of it. The only institutions appearing in top 500
institutions from India are Indian Institute of Sciences, Bangalore; IIT, Kharagpur and University of Calcutta. Even the
“five star” level by the National Assessment & Accreditation Council (NAAC) or considered as “potential centres of
excellence’ by the UGC does not find a place in top 500 universities except the University of Calcutta.
 
Action taken (5.1 and 5.2)
 
The observations have been noted.
 
The structure of governance varies in Universities and Deemed Universities. Any change in governance structures would
have be consistent with the appreciation of these institution being democratic institutions with collective decision
making bodies for both academics as well as administrative. The authenticity of world ranking of universities is not
known.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
5.6       Question of quality is also linked directly with the quality of teachers; curriculum design & development;
evaluation of teachers and students performance; teacher training; and other infrastructure such as good labs, libraries,
sports facilities, etc. Greater and regular sharing of experiences through networking and otherwise between different
institutions at the national and global plane is highly recommended. Multi-disciplinary curriculum with stress on
developing; problem-solving abilities, augmenting knowledge skill and group activities are essential to provide relevance
and usefulness to real life situations.   Quality of higher education can be greatly enhanced through the use of audio-
visual techniques and the modern information & communication technologies.
 
Action taken
 
Greater use of ICT is envisaged during the XIth Plan and the valuable observations of the Hon’ble Committee shall be
taken into consideration while finalizing the proposals for the Plan.
 
Recommendations/observations
 
5.7       Providing adequate exposure to teachers and students by holding more and more conferences and seminars,
orientation and refresher courses for teachers, making selection process of Lecturers/ Teachers/ Professors more
transparent and shifting from incremental budgeting to performance budgeting are some of the areas, the Committee
feels, if implemented, can go a long way in improving the quality and standard of higher education.
 
Action taken
 
The observations of Hon’ble Committee have been noted.

8.4       Private Universities
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
8.4.4    The Committee was cautioned that some corporate entities might try to open private universities to enhance their
profits under that garb. The possibility of a company opening a private university for the purpose of creating an
affiliating body to get all frivolous or sub-standard courses offered by it affiliated, cannot be ruled out. The Committee,
therefore, desires that the Government should bring a comprehensive legislation for providing effective machinery to
ensure that only genuine and quality private providers of higher education services remain in the field.
 
Action taken
 
According to the existing policy, only “Not for profit” societies or trusts can establish educational institutions.
 
8.5       Unaided Professional Institutions
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
8.5.5    These institutions, particularly in the field of engineering and management need to have effective partnership
with trade and industry to ensure that the product emerging out of these institutions would be better suited for the job
which they would eventually take up. Such a partnership, the Committee feels, shall not only make the curricula more
relevant and contextual, increase the employability of students and would also enable the sponsors to get some resources.
 
Action taken
 
The observations of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted.
 
XII.      State Universities
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
12.5     The Committee’s attention was also drawn towards the need for relaxing the requirement of NET qualification
for a person to be appointed as a Lecturer in a university/college because this sometimes prohibited the qualified and
outstanding persons from being inducted in the teaching community, if they have not cleared the NET. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that this issue needs to be considered by the Department and the UGC in a positive spirit.
 
Action taken
 
A review the National Eligibility Test (NET) for its utility, effectiveness and continuation was constituted by the Central
Government under the Chairmanship of Prof. B.L. Mungekar. Based on the recommendation contained in the Interim
Report of the Review Committee, the UGC has since notified the University Grants Commission Regulations for
(Minimum Qualifications Required for the Appointment and Career Advancement of Teachers in Universities and
Institutions Affiliated to it) (Second Amendment Regulations, 2006) on 14.6.2006. It has now been provided that the
candidates having Ph.D. degree in the concerned subjects are exempted from NET for Post Graduate level and Under
Graduate level teaching. The candidates having M.Phil degree in the concerned subjects are exempted from NET for UG
level teaching only.
 
XV.      Conclusion
 
Recommendations/observations
 
15.2     This Report, in fact, has attempted to suggest mechanisms/measures for taking most of the problems and
challenges, if not all, before higher education. The Committee is aware of the fact that doing all this would need huge

concerns relating to private funding were taken care of, the major share of the required money, the Committee feels, will
have to be primarily provided by the government. As per an estimate, nearly 3400 crores of rupees shall be required for
improving the infrastructure in the existing universities, filling vacancies of the teachers, upgrading the libraries and

mind on this issue. This investment should not be a big price for the benefits that would accrue to the country. Socio-
economic benefits of Higher education are immense and radiate to various areas of life.
 
Action taken
 
Based on the projection made by this Department on requirement for enhanced allocation for the Higher Education
sector, budgetary provision for the year 2006-07 has been increased from Rs.873.27 crores in 2005-06 to Rs.1403.50
crores.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE
IN VIEW OF GOVERNMENT'S REPLY
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.5       The Committee was informed that there are other ways also of looking at this access ratio which are given here as
follows:
 
(a)
     Percentage in terms of people in 18-23 age – 5-7 per cent
(b)     Percentage in terms of number appearing for class 12th – 30 - 35 per cent
(c)     Percentage in terms of number who has passed class 12th – 40-45 per cent
 
Action taken
 
The percentage in terms of people in the relevant age group (18-23 years) is estimated at 8.97 percent and is marginally
higher inclusive of enrolment in the Open and Distance Learning system of higher education.
 
3.13     Open University
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.13.2  The Committee believes that for a vast country like India where accessibility to higher education is quite low,
Open Universities have the vast potential for taking higher education to more and more people irrespective of different
barriers. This system caters also for in-service persons for whom it is a second chance as well as for regular learners.   It,
therefore, needs to be provided greater thrust by integrating utility courses with personal development and socio-
economic problems. The courses offered could be mainly job-oriented as far as possible. High priority should be given
for opening more study centres particularly covering rural and remote areas with concentration of SC/ST and other
backward communities’ students.
 
Action taken
 
The Open and Distance Learning format has been growing in terms of enrolment. The IGNOU offers a variety of job-
oriented courses. The DEC encourages State Open Universities (SOUs) also to introduce such courses with the opening
up of more and more study centers in backward areas and in scheduled areas, enrolment of weaker sections is expected

196thReport of Human Resource Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/196threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:42:40]
to increase.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.13.8  The Committee takes note of the fact that the open universities were able to raise some revenue by running
various courses offered through distance mode, there was no facility of fee concession available to eligible students in
the ODL system. The Committee finds such a system to be discriminatory. It feels strongly that the fees in this system
should also be rationalized and the poor and meritorious students be given some kind of fee concessions or assistance.
 
Action taken
 
While the fee in the ODL system is comparatively lower than in the conventional system, State Governments reimburse
Learners belonging to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes under scholarship schemes thus effectively providing
for concessional fee.
 
3.15     Women and Higher Education
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.15.4  Of the total women enrolled during 2004-05, as may be noted, more than 50 per cent were in Arts & Humanities.
Of the remaining 50 per cent, 20 per cent were in Sciences; 16 per cent in Commerce & Management; just 1.86 per cent
in education; 4.15 per cent in Engineering & Technology and 3.6 per cent in Medicine. The presence of women in
agriculture, mainstay of Indian economy, is just negligible. It is a matter of great concern that the participation of women
in the areas with great demand such as management, engineering/technology, medicine, etc. is very low in India. Such a
situation, the Committee feels, does not augur well for the future of this nation. Can a nation progress in real terms and
catch up with others in this fiercely competitive world with their women-folk remaining virtually outside the higher
education system? The Committee, therefore, recommends that the participation of women in professional courses,
which is abysmally low at present, needs to be improved manifold without further delay. More and more women as
Engineers, Professors, Lawyers, Doctors, Architects and Entrepreneurs could mould the face of India to a great extent.
 
Action taken
 
The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee would be kept in focus while formulating the XIth Plan.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.15.9  The open distance learning, the Committee feels, could be a very potent method to fight gender disability in
higher education. Studies in different areas may be promoted for women in user-friendly manner in the language they
prefer with suitable study materials. Training rural women for the purpose of involving them through community
participation in our development process should also be promoted. Their involvement in Sarva Siksha Abhiyan more
particularly the Mid-Day Meal 
could make these schemes a great success. For achieving these objectives, the Committee
is of the considered view, Government will have to play a pro-active, positive,  interventionist role to ensure access of all
eligible women to the higher education.
 
Action taken
 
The recommendations have been noted.
 
IV.       Relevance
 
Recommendations/observations
 
4.2      The Committee notes that the problem of relevance of higher education is mainly with reference to general
education i.e. Arts, Humanities & Social Science and Law & Commerce, wherein 83% of the 92 lakhs students, i.e. 76

lakhs are enrolled. However, in today’s new economic environment need for knowledge-workers and graduates with
sound fundamentals, good analytical abilities and appropriate utility-oriented skills are on rise and they are in great
demand. The Committee finds that most of our universities and colleges are providing out-dated, if not sub-standard
education in these disciplines, leading to the degrees and diplomas of little or no substance. The content as well as the
quality of education is mostly out of context and even if the curriculum is relevant, the teaching process is unscientific
and sub-optimal. Not only this, the Committee came to know that our institutions sometimes copy syllabi from Western

main reasons for increasing disinterest and frustration amongst the country’s youth. The Committee recommends that
the Government must take necessary measures, in consultation with experts, to ensure that required revision in the
content and curriculum is carried out periodically. It has to be in keeping with indigenous conditions and requirements.
There has to be an institutional mechanism to ensure that higher education remained relevant to the changing times.
Process of such revision, the Committee feels, should be an on-going one for making higher education relevant and
useful.
 
Action taken
 
As part of the UGC’s efforts to support teaching-learning innovations in various subjects, a model curriculum is prepared
from time to time by a panel of experts at the undergraduate and postgraduate levels for suitable adoption by the

Development Committees. Universities use the UGC Model Curriculum for upgrading their curriculum. This model
curriculum in all subjects has been circulated to all the Institutions for making higher education more relevant and
useful.
4.5
              Promoting Research
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
4.5.1    Research performance is one of the parameters of deciding world ranking of the universities. The fact that only
one of our universities finds place in top 500 universities of the world, speaks volumes about the status of research in our
country. The Committee finds that the research activities were not getting due attention in our universities, which should
have been one of their real basis. In fact, there have emerged the system of premier institutes and laboratories, both in
pure sciences and the social sciences and humanities, where research was moved away from our universities. As a result
of separation of research from teaching, the latter acquired gradually a secondary importance. The Committee, therefore,
is of the opinion that research needs to be closely linked with teaching for which scientific base in our universities needs
to be strengthened that will attract not only talented students but also industry to our university laboratories.
 
Action taken
 
An Expert Committee was constituted to suggest ways of strengthening basic science research in universities and to
attract talented students to basic sciences. The Report of the Committee has been accepted and is being implemented by
the UGC through an Empowered Committee of Experts. The main recommendations under implementation are:
 
i)          Filling up vacant faculty position.
ii)         No of Ph.D’s should increase.
 
The UGC has been advised to earmark allocation for implementation.

              Promoting Basic Sciences
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
4.6.1    Another worrisome fact that was brought to the notice of the Committee was the future of basic sciences in India.
It came to know that India’s best minds were not turning to pure and basic sciences and those who do not continue. The

science departments, not to speak of opening new institutions for imparting science education. The students have more
preference for courses in management, commerce, engineering, IT and related areas.
 
Action taken
 
Noted.
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
4.6.2    India has had a long tradition of pure sciences, the Committee is concerned to notice the increasing disinterest
among the younger generations in this area. It was mainly because of non-availability of suitable job opportunities and

integrate R&D activities in sciences with its economic and social programmes, because science must serve the socio-
economic and other needs of our society. Science & Technology has to play a greater role in prevention, mitigation and
management of the impact of natural disasters like earthquakes and Tsunamis. The Committee, therefore, feels that we
must find ways of making the study of pure as well as applied sciences, both in teaching & research, more attractive for
our students, if India were to use science for the welfare of its people. We must augment further our efforts in critical
areas like agricultural production, food processing, energy, transportation, communication, etc. so as to be able to

Recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted.

study of basic sciences more attractive. The Committee is of the view that all research institutes may also be persuaded

Recommendations/Observations
 
5.3       Such a situation, the Committee feels, does not augur well for the future of higher education in the country. The

A university can be established by an act of parliament or act of State legislature. There is no distinction under the

generally called a Private University.
 
8.5       Unaided Professional Institutions
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
8.5.1    The Country in recent years has witnessed emergence of self-financed institutions offering various courses in
engineering, medical, management, etc. That is mainly run by trusts and societies. Lakhs of enthusiastic men and women
have taken admission in these institutions. For example, if we take only engineering colleges, there was an intake of

more than 4 lakh students in 2004-2005 in the self-financed technical institutions scattered in different parts of the
country. The administrative and management structure of these institutions, the Committee came to know, was archaic.
While some of them are doing extremely well, others do not have even the basic infrastructure for the courses being
offered by them. Most of these institutions, the Committee was informed, suffered from acute shortage of qualified

Action taken
 
The observations of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted. The shortage of qualified teachers is owing to the
competing demands of the other sectors of the economy. The Central Government is constantly endeavoring to ensure
that talented young persons are attracted to the teaching profession. Several long term measure, including a review of the
remuneration packages are required to be considered. In the short term, the AICTE permits reappointment of teachers
upto the age of 70 years in order to meet the shortages in unaided institutions, subject to capacity of persons thus
appointed. The admission procedure as well as the fee structure in unaided educational institutions are indeed cause for
alertness. The Constitutions (93

Recommendations/observations
 
14.2     The UGC was established to promote, coordinate and determine standards in respect of higher education in the

III.       ACCESS AND EQUITY
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.3       The Committee observes that higher education in India was never freely available to all; it was basically elitist in
nature due mainly to historical and other reasons. Even after its expansion in post-Independence period, it could not be
made a mass activity.   Even today, it is neither fully accessible nor equitous. The Committee is of the opinion that the
issues of access & equity, in fact, are the two core issues to the expansion of higher education and hence, to the overall
progress of a nation. The Committee, therefore, underlines the urgent need for broadening access to higher education by
expanding it and by making it affordable.
 
3.4       The Committee is of the view that the two issues of access and equity are inextricably linked to one another.
There are two aspects of issue of access. Firstly, it can be looked as percentage of our young people (18-23 years) who
are eligible for higher education. Only close to seven per cent of our young people in this age-group today are in higher
education. The corresponding figure in the OECD countries is as high as 45-50 per cent and is over 90 per cent in
countries like Canada.
 
 
 
Action taken (3.3 and 3.4)
 
Concerns of Equity in access to Higher Education had not been adequately addressed until recently. The Constitution
(93
rd Amendment) Act, 2005 enables the Centre as well as the States to further conditions for success in higher
education in a manner that the weaker sections are not excluded from access to higher and technical education.
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee fails to understand the contention that the 93
rd Amendment alone could address the concerns of equity
and access to higher education. While this recommendation aimed at extending access to higher education to some
sections of the society, the Committee’s emphasis was for increasing access to all the sections of the society including
the weaker ones. The Committee would, therefore, like to have further comments of the Ministry on this aspect.

3.9       Regional Disparity
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.9.1    The Committee notes the conclusion of a study undertaken by a group of Indian scholars based in Japan and
USA, which had analyzed the funding of Higher education in different states by the Department. The study has shown
that Union Government’s expenditure on higher education to various states was grossly uneven. For example, last year’s
budget’s allocation for the states like Bihar, Rajasthan, Orissa, etc., was highly inadequate. Per person expenditure on
higher education in Bihar was Rs.1.87, in Rajasthan Rs.2.59 and in Orissa it was Rs.4.07 while in States like
Uttaranchal, it was Rs.105.42, in Arunachal Pradesh Rs.105 and in Assam Rs.77.7.
 
3.9.2    Another distinctive feature of regional disparity is visible in the number of colleges/institutions located in
different States. The four Southern States and Maharashtra having 32% of India’s population have 46% of total general
colleges and almost 60% of professional institutions. In contrast, in the States of UP, MP and Bihar (including
Jharkhand) having 34% of population, only 23% of general colleges and only 14% of professional colleges are located.
The Committee is concerned to see that in the most populous States where nearly ¾
th of our population lived, the access
ratio is far below the national average. It presents quite a dismal picture about the existing status of higher education in
the country.
 
3.9.3    The Committee strongly feels that there is an urgent need to remove this regional disparity.   It is high time that
Central Government takes some initiatives for encouraging and helping the State Governments to set up educational
institutions in tune with the global requirements.

While the Central Government is not aware of the authenticity of the said study mentioned by the Hon. Committee, it
may be mentioned that the Central Governments’ expenditure on higher education is mainly in respect of development

3.12
          System of affiliation
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
Another issue that Committee wishes to highlight is about system of affiliation.   In India most of its 16000 odd colleges
are affiliated ones. In the absence of proper facilities, many of these colleges perform only classroom teaching in a
traditional way. The Committee was informed that nearly 89 per cent of UG students, 66 per cent of PG students and 85
per cent of the faculty in higher educational institutions, were in these affiliated colleges. Consequently, the M.Sc., MA,
Ph.Ds that are coming out of such colleges are undoubtedly of poor quality. What is worse, in India major affiliating
universities are over-burdened with the administrative works which are unproductive in academic terms. The Committee
is of the view that this certainly telling upon the academic competence of our universities. The VCs of such universities
are left with no time for their academic pursuits. The Committee, therefore, recommends that there should be a cap on
the number of colleges being affiliated to a university. For this, we would need to open more and more universities for
which about 1000 universities and university level institutions be set up by 2015 in the Central, State and private sector.
A country like Japan, it may be noted, has around 700 universities and USA has nearly 3000 of them. Besides, setting up
more universities, we must encourage good colleges and institutions to acquire ‘deemed university’ or autonomous status
by fulfilling the norms laid down in this regard. This, the Committee feels, would not only lessen the burden of
universities but also enhance their quality and output greatly. Besides, the colleges should be encouraged to offer more
and more applied courses by offering job-oriented courses particularly after 10+2. These measures, if taken up in a
planned and fixed schedule would go a long way in decreasing the unnecessary burden on our universities.

3.14     Distance Education Council
 
Recommendations/Observations
 
3.14.1  The Distance Education Council (DEC) has been created under the IGNOU Act for the promotion and
coordination of Open University and distance education system and for the determination of its standard. The Committee
found that the opinion is divided on the power of the DEC to recognize/approve the courses/degrees being offered by the
various other universities/institutions in the country by distance mode. It is argued that the DEC having been created
under the Act of a university should not have such jurisdiction in respect of courses/degrees offered by the other
universities. It may be pointed that the DEC has been issuing notifications to universities asking them to get their
programmes approved quoting a particular Gazette Notification regarding students not being eligible for Central
Government jobs, if they pursue courses not approved by the DEC. Many of the universities are not prepared to accept

lines of AICTE or UGC.

by the Central Government. The Committee is happy to note the several initiatives taken by the DEC, such a common
pool of programmes, evolving common standards, system of credit transfer, etc.  The Committee is also of the view that
the DEC should be developed as an apex body for promoting, coordinating and determining standards in distance
education more or less on the lines of the UGC in the case of conventional education.

mode.

Orientation) of Education.  This was to ensure that the students at the first degree level develop knowledge, skills and
attitudes for gainful employment with emphasis on self-employment. Since 1994-95, a large number of colleges and

The Committee was informed that the UGC had allowed the system of earning certificate/diploma in utility-oriented

possibility of main degree neglected at the cost of utility-oriented one, as a result, a student may not be able to show his

5.10     Assessment & Accreditation
 
Recommendations/observations
 
5.10.1  The National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC) was established by the UGC in 1994 to assess the
quality and accredit universities and colleges depending upon certain specified parameters/indicators. The Committee
was however, informed that even after almost two decades, the process of assessment and accreditation has not had the
desired impact. Hardly 10 to 15% of the total higher & technical education institutions have gone through this process
mainly due to inadequate infrastructure and other weaknesses in the NAAC.
 
5.10.2  A major weakness in the existing institutional assessment, the Committee notes, is that while it assesses the
performance of the university or colleges as a whole; it does not do it Department-wise. What is known to the people is
the grades and stars, which signify only averages. Academic performance of a university, in fact, is mostly department-
specific. As a result, weaker ones are not exposed. Therefore, the idea of grouping them together for assessment, the
Committee feels, needs to be reconsidered. The Committee recommends that the NAAC should start accrediting
individual departments also of a university in addition to its overall grading, at the earliest.
 
5.10.3  The Committee was informed that accreditation being voluntary, many institutions that have secured
accreditation may not turn up for re-accreditation after five years and may still continue to use the grade obtained earlier.
Others do not turn up for accreditation at all. The Committee is aware that it would be difficult to enforce, if
accreditation is made mandatory. The Committee proposes, as incentive for this purpose, that the accreditation must be
linked with the grants or special assistance/recognition by the UGC and other bodies so that institutions turn up for
accreditation. In USA, the Committee learnt, federal grants are available only to the accredited institutions.
 
5.10.4  The Committee was informed that the process and procedure of assessment and accreditation by the NAAC takes
a long time. It, therefore, emphasizes the urgent needs to identify efficient ways and effective strategies for expediting
the assessment and accreditation by NAAC within a stipulated time frame.
 
5.10.5  The Committee learnt that parameters adopted by the NAAC for evaluating the quality, although useful, leave
some scope for subjectivity in this exercise. The Committee recommends that this aspect should be re-examined with a
view to making these parameters transparent and objective.
 
5.10.6  The Committee also underlines the greater need for evolving an internal self-regulatory quality assurance
mechanism by the accredited institutions for maintaining and upgrading their quality level. This mechanism may also
monitor both academic excellence as well as administrative efficiency of that institution. Periodic assessment of
accredited institution should also be carried out regularly by the NAAC.
 
5.10.7  The Committee, in view of the emerging scenario, is of the opinion that a Government agency like NAAC for
assessment of standards and accreditation of higher educational institutions may not have the desired
credibility/acceptability to our higher education institutions at the international level. In fact, the need for a third party
evaluation model with participation of all the stakeholders in higher education was underlined by some experts who
appeared before the Committee. The Committee also feels that the establishment of an independent accreditation agency
having regional offices in different areas of the country should also be considered. The industry should also have its

196thReport of Human Resource Development
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/196threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:42:40]
participation in such a machinery. It should be, more or less, on the lines of quality assurance bodies like ISO and other
rating agencies like CRISIL and ICRA.
 
Action taken (5.10.1 to 5.10.7)
 
The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee are noted. There is an urgent need for giving a new orientation and
thrust to the functioning of NAAC so that it could meet the emerging challenges in the higher education system. Keeping
this in view, the Government had recently constituted a three-member Expert Committee to review the functioning of
NAAC. The said Committee has since submitted its report to the Ministry and some of the suggestions made by the said
Committee largely address the concern expressed by the Hon’ble Committee. In order to develop a credible, acceptable
and transparent accreditation process, the Experts have recommended identification of quality parameters and conversion
of scores obtained individually by the institution for each parameter, for computing overall grading of the institution, be
done with great care and clarity. The NAAC has attempted to modify the instrument of assessment with introduction of
key indicators. It has also modified the peer teams selection process which are now selected by computerized random
selection process from a panel approved by a Sub-Committee of the Executive Council of NAAC. Further, a series of
training programmes are also being organized by NAAC to minimize the scope for subjective peer judgment. The
NAAC has been advocating in-house mechanism called Internal Quality Assurance Cell (IQAC) to be established in all
accredited institutions and the same has been made mandatory requirement for the institutions opting for re-
accreditation. The report of the Expert Committee also envisages continuation of active post accreditation process to
maintain certain standards for the institutions. The recommendations of the Expert Committee are presently under
consideration of the Government. 
 
Comments of the Committee (5.10.1 to 5.10.7)
 
The Committee is informed that the MHRD had constituted an Expert Committee to review the functioning of the

and the UGC has been advised to initiate necessary follow-up action on the recommendations in a time bound manner.
The Committee would like to have a brief status note about these recommendations and the action taken by the UGC.

6.         Governance and Management
 
Recommendations/observations
 
6.2       With major interventions by the State for universalisation of education, latest being the SSA and MDM, the
Committee feels, the secondary and then the higher secondary education is bound to face in the coming years
unprecedented pressure of numbers as well as quality. Besides, the emerging new regime under GATS has also posed
newer challenges before higher education. Such a situation calls for a modern system of management for the higher
education to enable India to compete and survive at the global level. The Committee feels that our universities and
institutions of higher learning should be prepared to respond to such demands and challenges, and this cannot be done
without making suitable changes in the system of governance and administrative structures of higher education in the
country.
 
Action taken
 
Observations of the Hon’ble Committee have been noted.
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee is not at all satisfied with the reply of the MHRD. It would like to know as to what specific steps are
being taken to meet the challenges before higher education today. The Committee would also like to be apprised of the
changes made/being made in the system of governance and administrative structures of higher education in the country.
 
Recommendations/observations
 
6.3       The Committee notes that management in education though not unknown in India, works more or less, on old
structure and concepts. It is a matter of concern that most of our universities have become merely examination boards for
conducting examinations and conferring degrees, apart from the major work of granting affiliations. The Committee is
dismayed to note that research as well as pedagogical innovations seems to have taken a back seat in the universities.
The Committee is of the considered opinion that in such a scenario what is needed is the greater autonomy,
professionalism, transparency and accountability in the administration of higher education.
 
Action taken
 
The current policy of the government is to encourage autonomy of institutions of higher learning.  
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee is of the considered opinion that encouraging autonomy of institutions of higher learning alone may not
suffice. The MHRD has to evolve a more relevant system based on modern management techniques whereby
professionalism, transparency and accountability in the administration of higher education could be ensured.
 
Recommendations/observations

been given to understand that State Governments are being regularly requested by UGC to institute criminal proceedings
against fake institutions. Even UGC has also decided to take action. The Committee would, however, like to point out
that criminal proceedings will not make any difference in the status of such institutions due to the continuation of very
mild penalty provisions.

13.2     The Committee understands that pursuant to the recommendations of the Committee on Petitions (Lok Sabha), a
Bill was introduced in the Rajya Sabha in December, 1991 providing for imprisonment upto six months and a fine of not
less than Rs.1 lakh which may extend to Rs.10 lakhs. This Bill was subsequently withdrawn on 1 st June, 1995.
Thereafter, no further project seems to have been made on such a vital issues.  The Committee would like to emphasize
that urgent steps need to be taken for bringing a legislation providing for more stringent penalties for running fake
universities.
 
 
Action taken (13.1 and 13.2)
 
The legislative provisions as they exist on-date are not adequate to check fake Universities functioning in contravention
of the University Grants Commission Act, 1956. The UGC has also approached the concerned State Governments to
prosecute the offenders and to take appropriate punitive action under the India Penal Code. The UGC has been advised
to give wide publicity using all available and effective media to bring out the facts about such institutions to the notice of
public and the student community, including the UGC’s website, cautioning aspiring students against seeking admission
in, or dealing with, such fake institutions. In addition, the Government is contemplating a comprehensive review of the
University Grants Commission Act, 1956 including the existing provision for action against those indulging in fake
educational activities.
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee has been reiterating for the last so many years the need for taking urgent steps for bringing a legislation
providing for more stringent penalties for running fake universities. The Committee is, however, constrained to observe
that this problem would perhaps continue to persist, simply because the exercise of comprehensive review of the UGC
Act, 1956 is still being contemplated by the Government. The Committee would once again impress upon the
Department not to further delay this crucial issue.

Recommendations/observations
 
15.1     In view of the new situations and the resulting challenges before higher education in the emerging scenario, the
need for preparing ourselves to face them successfully brooks no delay. India will have to take various measures, legal,
institutional, financial and others well in time so that we are not left behind in this fast changing world. For this, there is
an urgent need for reform and revitalization of education sector to make it relevant and suitable to the emerging socio-
economic and other realities. The National Policy on Education that was formulated nearly two decades ago even before
the process of liberalization had begun, the Committee feels, needs to be revisited with a view to making it more
forward-looking and vibrant. The new concerns also will have to be included in it. Besides, the existing legal framework
in the higher education sector particularly, the UGC Act and the Acts of various State Universities also need to be make
more relevant and effective in the present context.

rd) on the subject.

PART - I
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS EITHER ACCEPTED BY THE DEPARTMENT OR HAVING BEEN
SATISFACTORILY REPLIED TO BY THE DEPARTMENT
 
II.         NORMS FOR OPENING OF KENDRIYA VIDYALAYAS
 
Recommendations/Observation
2.1       Opening of Kendriya Vidyalayas is based on specific norms prescribed for this purpose by the Govt.  One of those
was the provision of 15 acres of land to be provided free of cost by the sponsoring agencies.  The Committee was informed
that this criterion had now been drastically reduced to 4.00 acres in a metropolitan city; a contiguous plot fairly leveled
measuring 6.00 acres in hilly terrain; 8.00 acres in urban area; and 10.00 acres in rural/semi urban area.  The Committee
appreciates that in view of the ever-increasing shortage of land in the present scenario, lowering the land requirement is
the need of the hour.  However, the Committee would like to emphasize that there should be no deviation from the need to
demarcate 40% as building area and 60% as play field of the 4.00 acres provided in a metropolitan city.
 
Action Taken
As suggested by the Committee due consideration is being given by KVS to demarcate 40% of the land for
building area and 60% as play field.
 
IV.       KENDRIYA VIDYALAYA BUILDINGS
Recommendations/Observations
4.3       The Committee observes that considerable time is taken in the various stages of construction including the delay,
sometimes, at the planning stage. What is more disturbing is that a large number of these KVs, has been opened way back
in eighties. The Committee understands that after a protracted procedure involving States/sponsoring agencies and
overcoming a number of hurdles, these KVs must have reached the stage when finally construction project could be
sanctioned. However, it appears that series of other procedural formalities are yet to be fulfilled, before the students could
pursue their studies in a proper environment having required infrastructure.
 
Recommendations/Observations
4.4       The Committee found that construction of another 28 school buildings was at the planning stage. The Committee
finds that these KVs are scattered in different State of the country, having various sponsoring agencies. The Committee is
concerned to note that out of these 28 KVs, no progress is expectedin 19 KVs, due to various reasons beyond the control
of KV Sangathan. In some cases construction agencies have not submitted even preliminary drawings and estimates. They
are reminded from time to time to expedite it. In such a situation the Committee is constrained to conclude that the
construction status of these KVs would continue to remain at the same stage. It appears that no agency is responsible and
KV Sangathan itself seems to have abdicated its responsibility/duty.
 
Action Taken
(4.3 & 4.4)
KVS works are being executed  through Govt. construction agencies as a “Deposit Work”, in which construction
agencies are responsible for planning, designing and execution of work as per their execution system of public work.
KVS’s role is to monitor the progress and release funds accordingly. In case of any hurdle and delay, KVS takes up the
matter with the Heads/site staff of concerned construction agencies. For proper and effective monitoring, review

197thReport of Human Resource Development

meetings/discussions are being made at various levels i.e.: -
(i)         Works Committee Meeting – under the Chairmanship of Joint  Secretary, HRD/Vice-Chairman, KVS – to review
the progress and other related problems.
(ii)        Review of works by Commissioner, KVS, with the Head of construction agency.
(iii)       Monthly review meetings at KVS level.
(iv)       Monitoring at Region level.
(v)        Monitoring at Vidyalaya level by Vidyalaya Monitoring Committee.
After transfer of suitable plot of land to a KV, construction works are entrusted to the Govt. construction agencies
and these are chased up regularly for submitting the drawings & estimate for issuing Admn. Approval and Exp. Sanction.
After the sanction is issued, Construction agency is regularly chased for early start of work by completing pre-tender
planning in time. On account of close monitoring as many as 32 school buildings have been got completed during this
period.
 
Recommendations/Observations
4.5       The Committee made an attempt to understand the factors primarily responsible for such a dismal situation with a
view to find a solution to break this impasse. The Committee summoned the DG, CPWD to discuss this problem as also to
understand his constraints. The Committee was given to understand that KV Sangathan has a well laid-out monitoring
mechanism functioning at different levels. The Committee, however, feels that this monitoring mechanism has not proved
to be very effective so far. The Committee observes that an initiative has been taken to simplify procedural formalities.
Henceforth, all sanction orders issued by KVS are to be forwarded to the concerned CPWD authorities by name. This
would result in eliminating undue delay occurring at various levels in KVS as well as in CPWD.
Action Taken
As regards, issuing of sanction order are concerned these are already being forwarded to the Heads of concerned
construction agency. However it is noted for compliance that in future all sanction orders will be issued by name to the
concerned authorities of CPWD.
 
Recommendations/Observations
4.6       Another problem noticed by the Committee was lack of co-ordination between the civil and electrical wings of
CPWD. This also, the Committee found, leads to unnecessary delays in this regards. The Committee is happy to note that
CPWD has since introduced a composite tendering system, where under electrical works inside the building are to be made
part of the main contract.
 
Action Taken
In the sanction order of school building project, KVS has already incorporated a clause of executing the work
through a composite tender.
PART-II
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS ON WHICH COMMITTEE HAS FURTHER COMMENTED UPON.
 
II.         NORMS FOR OPENING OF KENDRIYA VIDYALAYAS
 
Recommendations/Observations
2.2       The Committee came to know that out of 931 KVs in the country, there are 38 KVs where land had not been
provided by the sponsoring agencies even after several years, which in some cases is more than 20 to 25 years.  In the case
of as many as 27 KVs, sponsoring agencies were the Armed Forces.  The Committee notes that with the exception of two
KVs opened in the year, 2005-06, rest were opened between 1977-78 to 1997-98.  In the remaining 11 KVs also the
situation was, more or less, the same; the earliest KV was opened in 1973-74.  Details of such KVs reveal a very
discouraging picture.   The Committee hopes that with the revision of land norms, situation would improve.  The
Committee would like the Department of Secondary & Higher Education and KVS to vigorously pursue the allotment of
land with the concerned agencies and report the progress made in this regard to the Committee within three months.
 
Action Taken
Following efforts have been made to obtain land from the sponsoring agencies:
 
a)         The issues have been discussed by Ministry of Human Resource Development with concerned State Govt.
representatives in the regional level meetings.

197thReport of Human Resource Development

b)         Meetings have been held by KVS with  Ministries of Home Affairs, Finance & Defence.
c)         A series of D.O letters have been addressed by Commissioner to Officers of concerned Ministries of Government
of India and Chief Secretaries of States. As on date out of 919 functional KVs, land is yet to be provided in respect
of 126 KVs of which 35 cases are pending with Ministry of Defence, 8 with State Govts, and 12 with Ministries of
Home, Finance and Railways.  The present position of the 38 cases mentioned by the Committee is at Annexure-I.
 
Comments of the Committee
The Committee had identified 38 Kendriya Vidyalayas where land had not been made available by the sponsoring
agencies even after a lapse of 20-25 years in some cases.  The latest status report in respect of these 38 Kendriya
Vidyalayas reveals that position remains unchanged.  Correspondence/meetings at different levels with all concerned have
not yielded any desired results.  The Committee observes that in most of the cases although land had been finally
earmarked by the sponsors, approval of the Ministry of  Defence / concerned State Government was awaited. The
Committee had called for a status report on this within three months.  The Committee is, however, constrained to note that
it is already more than six months since the presentation of its report, but there is no indication of any noticeable progress. 
The Committee takes a serious view of this.  The Committee is of the firm view that it is high time that the matter is taken
up at the highest level, be it the Ministry of Defence or any State Government.
The Committee observes that land is to be provided in respect of total 126 KVs.  38 KVs pointed out by the
Committee were the longest pending ones.  The Committee is of the view that with the relaxation in  land norms for
different areas, sponsoring agencies for KVs should be in a better position to provide the land.  The Committee,
accordingly, recommends that sponsoring agencies for all such KVs should be pursued vigorously for release of land in a
time-bound manner.
 
Recommendations/Observations
2.3       Besides the provision of land, the other basic criteria for opening a new KV is the availability of 200 children (500
in big cities) and minimum concentration of 1000 Central Government employees. In all the cases, proposal has to
emanate from State Government/Departments/Ministries/Defence authorities/PSUs.  Committee’s attention has been
drawn towards the opening of 98 KVs in a short span of two  years, i.e. during 2003-2004 and 2004-2005.  On a specific
query in this regard, the Committee was informed that only three KVs - two in the project sector and another one in Tehran
were opened on specific requests/proposals.  As regards the remaining 95, the Committee noticed a very disturbing aspect. 
In the normal course, demands for opening of a new KVs come from various sources, ranging from the elected
representatives to the State/project authorities.   However, the Committee was informed that these 95 KVs were opened
without there being a formal proposal from the KV Sangathan. These KVs were opened on communications received from
the then Chairman, KV Sangathan at different points of time. Opening of these KVs was apparently justified by the
availability of surplus teachers and need for utilizing their services.  The Committee was given to understand that ex-post
facto approval was proposed to be obtained from the Cabinet after the matter was discussed and approved in EFC
meeting.  That could, however, not be done.
 
Recommendations/Observations
2.4       The Committee takes a serious view of this development because the prescribed pre-sanction procedure for the
purpose was simply given a go by in these cases.  The Committee is perturbed to note that these 95 KVs were opened
without taking any prior approval/sanction.   Even the ex-post facto approval could not be taken.   The committee is not
happy with such an approach of short circuiting the established procedures.  In this case, in the absence of any formal
approval and their being no fund allocation specifically for these KVs plan funds are utilised to fulfill the salary and other
requirements of staff members, of these KVs.  This is not a healthy fiscal practice.
 
Action Taken
(Para 2.3&2.4)
The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs in its meeting held on 16.6.2006 has accorded ex-post facto approval
for opening of 95 Kendriya Vidyalayas opened during the years 2003-04 and 2004-05.Henceforth, it will be ensured by
KVS that orders for opening of new K.Vs are being issued only after obtaining necessary approval of Cabinet Committee
on Economic Affairs.
 
Comments of the Committee
(para 2.3 & 2.4)
The Committee in its 162
nd  Report presented on the 28th April, 2005 had commented upon the opening of 95 KVs
(64 in 2003-04 and 31 in 2004-05) in violation of norms, without sanction either by the Government or the Executive

197thReport of Human Resource Development

Committee of KVS.  The Committee was then given to understand that Government was contemplating to seek the
approval of the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) for continuation of these 95 KVs.  The Committee is
surprised to see that it took  more than a year for getting a formal approval of CCEA on the 16th June, 2006.  The
Committee hopes that the Department would abide by the assurance of opening of new KVs  henceforth only after
obtaining the necessary approval from CCEA.
 
Recommendations/Observations
2.5       The Committee is of the view that the role of the Government should be to ensure that prescribed norms for
opening of new KVs were strictly adhered to.  Instead of giving priority to such districts where KVs are genuinely required
and where there are no KVs, setting up such schools arbitrarily is certainly deplorable.
 
Action Taken
Recently after the approval of Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs, orders for opening of 50 new KVs have
been issued in such Districts, which fall under the criteria of Special Focus Districts having no KV.
 
Comments of the Committee    
The Committee appreciates the initiative taken by the Department for opening of 50 new Kendriya Vidyalayas in
special Focus Districts having no KVs.  The Committee would, however, like to impress upon the Department to play a
pro-active role in making these 50 new KVs functional at the earliest.
 
Recommendations/Observations

Action Taken
At present out of 95 KVs opened during 2003-04 and 2004-05, 86 KVs are functional. One reason for surplus of
teachers is withdrawal of some sections in some vidyalayas. Besides the work load of teachers has also changed.Only 6

Comments of the Committee    
Committee has been monitoring the status of 95 KVs opened during 2003-04 and 2004-05 (64 in 2003-04 and 31 in

non-provision of required infrastructure facilities by the concerned District Administration.   As per the latest status note

Recommendations/Observations
2.7       Details about schools made available to the Committee clearly indicate that enrolment status in some of the
Vidyalayas was far from satisfactory.   The Committee would like to emphasize that the Department ought to have been

more concerned about the present status of these schools; availability of required teachers and infrastructure; and also
about the number of students enrolled.  It recommends that the remedial steps be taken urgently to remove all the
shortcomings.  The Committee emphasizes the need to review these cases expeditiously.   In some cases even there is no

The present status of enrolment in 86 functional KVs are at Annexure-II. Efforts are continuously being made to

Comments of the Committee    
Committee's attention has been drawn by the increase in the student intake of these 84 functional KVs.  As
compared to earlier enrolment figures of 25,989 students, the latest details given to the Committee indicate that there are

infrastructure support.  The Committee notes that only 6 KVs are having XIth and XIIth class and the remaining KVs are
running either upto Xth class or below Xth class.  The Committee feels that with a large number of students completing
Xth class, a need would arise for adjusting them in XIth class.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Department should take up with concerned authorities for provision of required infrastructure, wherever feasible.   The
Committee is not aware whether land has been made available in respect of any of these KVs by the sponsoring
authorities.  Every effort needs to be made to expedite the process of land procurement so as to provide all the required

III.       PROJECT VIDYALAYAS
Recommendations/Observations
3.1       Committee’s attention was drawn towards the closure of a large number of project Vidyalayas due to failure of the
sponsoring agencies in providing the required funds.  The Committee reiterates that the Department and KVS should
approach the project authorities for re-opening of closed Vidyalayas.   Those Project Vidyalayas which could not be
revived may be taken over by the Government and run as normal KVs.
 
Action Taken
Budgetary allocations are given to KVS by the Ministry to manage the affairs of KVs which are opened with its
approval in the civil/defence sector. KVS is not given any funds from the Government to run Project Sector Vidyalayas.
Hence, the Project Authorities are expected to make available the required funds to re-open the KVs under Project Sector.
 
Comments of the Committee    
The Committee feels that the Department has not given much thought on the recommendations of the Committee
that those project vidyalayas which could not be revived may be taken over by the Government and run as normal
Kendriya Vidyalayas.  The Committee reiterates that the Department should approach the project authorities for reopening
of closed Vidyalayas.  At the sametime, wherever feasible, the Department should explore the possibility of taking over
those closed KVs which cannot be revived.  Basic idea behind this observation of the Committee was to make optimum
and judicious utilization of existing infrastructure/ facilities at these closed project Vidyalayas for the ultimate benefit of
our students.    
 
Recommendations/Observations
3.2       The Committee notes that there are 129 project sector KVs functioning at present. Outstanding dues amounting to

 V.       ADMISSION CRITERIA FOR STUDENTS
Recommendations/Observations
5.1       The Committee notes that the present admission policy results in overcrowding of certain KVs in different parts of
the country and it therefore, feels that this problem needs to be tackled without any further delay. In this regard,
Committee’s attention has been drawn by the Report of the Baldev Mahajan Committee given in 2000. One of the main
recommendations of the Mahajan Committee, the Committee as informed was that freezing of sections was neither
academically sound nor administratively feasible. The Committee is also of the view that problem of increasing number of
students cannot be solved by the freezing of sections. The Committee was also informed that the Board of Governors of
KV Sangathan was in agreement with the recommendation of the Baldev Mahajan Committee that the Commissioner,
KVS should have full powers of opening of new sections and sanctioning additional staff. The Board of Governors had,
accordingly, decided to recommend the same to the Government. The Committee, however, finds that as per the latest
response received from the Department, the recommendations of the Baldev Mahajan Committee have since been rejected
in principle. The Committee fails to comprehend the reasons for the change in the stand of the Government. The
Committee would like to point out that number of students in a class/section being more than the prescribed ratio, does
affect the quality of education adversely; it needs to be avoided. The Committee is also in favour of more and more
students getting admitted to the KVs. But overcrowding is certainly not conducive for focused attention on students’
performance. KVs cannot be an exception to this. The Committee, therefore, feels that all efforts need to be made to avoid
overcrowding in KVs by opening additional sections with all the infrastructure wherever needed.
 
Action Taken
Kendriya Vidyalayas primarily provide education to the wards of the transferable Central Govt. employees. These
employees get transferred to various metropolis and Kendriya Vidyalayas located in these cities/ state capitals have to
accommodate the children producing Transfer Certificate from another Kendriya Vidyalaya. One of the reasons of
overcrowding in KVs located in cities/state capitals is due to this factor. Use of special dispensation quota and demand
from Government employees for some centrally located KVs has put additional pressure. However, to ease the situation
new sections have been sanctioned in most of the KVs where infrastructure is available. To accommodate more students,
KVS has already started running of two shifts in 44 Kendriya Vidyalayas. In these KVs the problem of overcrowding has
eased to a certain extent. However, sections cannot be opened indiscriminately due to constraint of land and building
space. Within the capacity of the infrastructure, new sections are opened by KVS depending on need.
 
Comments of the Committee
The Committee has been expressing its concern about certain problems faced in implementing the discretionary
quota for the Members of Parliament for admission in the Kendriya Vidyalayas.  One such problem relates to those
Members of the Lok Sabha who do not have Kendriya Vidyalaya in their constituencies.   As per the existing system, they,
of course, get the prescribed coupons but cannot recommend any admission under this quota.  It, thus, amounts to denying
this facility to such MPs.  The Committee, therefore, feels that this lacunae needs to be corrected immediately by allowing
MPs under this category either to recommend admission in a school situated in the neighbouring  constituencies or
anywhere in their State, as is the case with the Members of the Rajya Sabha.

6.1       In its 162
nd Report, the Committee had dealt with the problem of vacancies existing in different categories of

alleged to have been committed, continued to remain undecided till September 2006.  As a result, the appointment of the
teachers was withheld.   In the meantime, a Satyam Committee was appointed to look into the issues and the selected
teachers were given conditional appointment on ad hoc basis, till the Committee submitted its report.  Thus, the teachers
remained ad-hoc for more than three years.  In the meanwhile, the Committee learnt that the report of the Satyam
Committee has since been submitted to the Government.   The Committee notes with serious concern that the process of
selection of teachers that had started in February 2003, could not be completed till the time of the writing of this Report. 
The Committee is at a loss to see that 1571 posts of teachers continued to remain vacant for several years.  The
Committee, while appreciating the move for giving the ad hoc appointment to the selected teachers pending the inquiry,

Recommendations/Observations
6.2       The Committee in its 162
nd Report had strongly advocated the need for having a decentralized – zone wise
recruitment for KV teachers, instead of the existing centralized procedure. The most obvious reason for having a
decentralization system is to avoid the inherent problems faced in a centralized recruitment system by the KVS and the
candidates coming from different part of such a vast country.  The Committee is of the firm view that centralized
recruitment system is of the main reasons for continuance of vacancies for long time affecting the academic environment
of the Vidyalayas.  The Committee therefore, reiterates its recommendations of decentralization of the recruitment process
for selection of candidates at zonal level so that it becomes convenient to people of different regions to participate in the
process which otherwise may not be possible for them.   It would also ensure proper representation of the candidates from
different parts of the country, particularly from NE States and J&K.
 
Action Taken
Prior to 1999 the direct recruitments to the teaching posts used to be made by short-listing the candidates on the
basis of pre-determined evaluation criteria taking into consideration the academic and professional achievements and co-
curricular activities followed by interviews.  Direct recruitment for the post of PRT, TGT and Misc. categories of teachers
was done at the regional level by constituting Selection Board.  Promotions to the aforesaid posts from feeder grades/ posts
used to be done centrally at the Hqrs.  The appointment of selected candidates was also done within the region.  The
promotions as well as appointment by direct recruitment of PGTs, Vice-principals and Principals were made centrally at
the HQ. level.  In this system while the candidates from the universities that give liberal marks used to get included in the
short-lists, while the relatively better candidates from the universities who do not give liberal marks could not make to the
lists.  In order to remove such disparities, it was decided on the recommendations of the Selja Committee to hold the
written examination to assess the real potential and capabilities of the candidates irrespective of the university or
institution from which they were coming.  Need was felt for centralization in the recruitment process in order to ensure
greater degree of objectivity, transparency, uniformity in standards and selection of teachers on the basis of proven merit
as independently assessed on a uniform and standard criteria. It was, therefore, decided to centralize the recruitment of all
teaching and non-teaching posts except Group ‘D’.   In the new system, all candidates who possess the requisite
qualifications prescribed for the post are required to take written examination and based on merit list, drawn on the basis of
their performance in written test & interviews, select panels are prepared.   The matter on decentralization of recruitments
was sent to Legal Adviser of KVS for his opinion.   He opined that the regional recruitment system if followed would lead
to innumerable litigations, as KVS cannot shut out outsiders from applying for any post.  It has been the experience of
KVS in the past that regional recruitment led to a lot of complications resulting in switching over to centralized
recruitment system. In KVS, posts are filled up on transfer also and if regional recruitment is resorted to and if posts are
filled up on transfer, disgruntled    persons approach the courts questioning the manner of filling up of posts.  Courts do
quash such filling up of posts by transfer.       So far as the representations of the candidates from different parts of the
country particularly from NE states and J&K are concerned, it is submitted that the advertisement for recruitment of
teachers is published in the Employment News (Weekly), National News papers and also in the local/vernacular News
Papers. Besides this each and every information relating to recruitment is uploaded on the website of KVS.  The

publication and displaying on notice boards of the Regional Offices as well as in the Schools is also taken at length for

apply in response to Sangathan’s advertisement.  In fact teachers working in the Kendriya Vidyalayas belong to all parts of

Comments of the Committee
(Para 6.1 & 6.2)
The Committee does not agree with the arguments given by the Department against decentralization of recruitment
