V.    ADMISSION CRITERIA FOR STUDENTS
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee has been expressing its concern about certain problems faced in implementing the discretionary
quota for the Members of Parliament for admission in the Kendriya Vidyalayas.  One such problem relates to those
Members of the Lok Sabha who do not have Kendriya Vidyalaya in their constituencies.   As per the existing system, they,
of course, get the prescribed coupons but cannot recommend any admission under this quota.  It, thus, amounts to denying
this facility to such MPs.  The Committee, therefore, feels that this lacunae needs to be corrected immediately by allowing
MPs under this category either to recommend admission in a school situated in the neighbouring  constituencies or
anywhere in their State, as is the case with the Members of the Rajya Sabha.       (Para 5.1)
 
VI.   VACANCY POSITION
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee does not agree with the arguments given by the Department against decentralization of recruitment
by Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan; it appears to be purely technical without appreciating the Committee’s concern.  The
Committee therefore, reiterates its recommendations for making decentralized recruitment in Kendriya Vidyalayas.  Steps
must be taken for removing the legal hurdles by framing suitable laws and regulations.                               (Para 6.1 & 6.2)
 
VII.      GRIEVANCES REDRESSAL
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee is not convinced with the Grievances redressal mechanism working in KVS, since there are no
details about the complaints received/ pending / redressal made during the last years. Without any supporting data, the
Committee is not able to judge the efficacy of the mechanism.                                            (Para 7.1)
 
VIII.     SURVEY OF KVs
 
Comments of the Committee
 
The Committee has been informed that an evaluation of KVs was conducted by a Committee under the
Chairmanship of Shri J.C. Pant, former Secretary to Government of India in 2002.  The Committee is not aware about the
mandate and area of evaluation of the Pant Committee.   A copy of the report of this Committee has also not been made
available to the Committee.  Against this backdrop, the stand taken by the Department that need for another evaluation of
KVs will be assessed by them is not acceptable to the Committee.   The Committee would also like to point out that
evaluation and survey are two different aspects.  The Committee therefore recommends that detailed survey of KVs as per
Committee's recommendation should be undertaken and completed at the earliest.                             (para 8.1 & 8.2)

REPORT
 
The Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Government on the recommendations contained in
its One Hundred Eighty-fourth report on "Major Issues concerning Navodaya Vidyalayas" of the Department of School
Education & Literacy.  The Committee had presented the Hundred and Fifty-fourth Report, a detailed analysis of various
aspects concerning the functioning of Navodaya Vidyalayas, to Lok Sabha on 2 nd March and Rajya Sabha on 3 rd March,
2005.  While considering the Action Taken Note on the Report received from the Department of Secondary and Higher
Education (now Department of School Education and Literacy) the Committee noticed that further clarifications were
required on a number of important issues.  The Committee accordingly, held another series of extensive deliberations with
all concerned and presented another Report (184
th) on the subject.
2.         While going through the Action Taken Notes received from the Department in respect of the
recommendations contained in the 184 th Report, the Committee observed that while in respect of some aspects, position
had considerably improved, there still remained some problem-areas where the Department was required to be pro-active.
Present Report has been accordingly divided into two parts.  Part-I deals with Recommendations/Observations either
accepted by the Department or having been satisfactorily replied to by the Department. Part-II relates to those
recommendations/observations on which Committee has further commented upon.

I.          NORMS FOR OPENING OF NAVODAYA VIDYALAYAS
Recommendations/Observations
1.2       Committee is concerned about the oft-repeated excuse given by the Department regarding the non-functional JNVs
i.e. non-availability of temporary accommodation that is to be provided by the State Governments.  The Committee is
perturbed over the non-challant attitude of the Government in making the JNVs functional.  The Committee strongly feels
that this being a Central Scheme, the JNV Samiti and the Department of Secondary & Higher must try to see that a
sanctioned JNV becomes functional as soon as possible and it must not be left to the States and wait till they take a
decision.  It is a scheme for the benefit of their students.  States, therefore, must be persuaded/advised and facilitated to
arrange an accommodation.
Action Taken
            The Ministry and NVS are regularly pursuing the matter with the Education Secretaries/Chief Secretaries of the

States to make available land and temporary accommodation.
            The temporary accommodation has since been made available since the last meeting for the following JNVs, which
have started functioning: -

2.      Deogarh (Orissa)
3.      Hamirpur (UP)
4.      Ghaziabad (UP)
5.      Rohtas (Bihar)

Land has also been transferred in respect of following JNVs and construction of buildings has been sanctioned.

2.      Anand (Gujarat)
3.      Jamtara (Jharkhand)
4.      Aizawal (Mizoram)
5.      Kolasib (Mizoram)
6.      Chimtuipui (Lawngtlai) (Mozoram)
7.      Lunglaei (Mizoram)
8.      Sarawasti (Uttar Pradesh)
9.      Ambedkar Nagar (Uttar Pradesh)
10.  Dehradun (Uttranchal)
Recommendations/Observations
1.6       Another issue connected with the scheme of Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalaya is shifting of the Navodaya Vidyalayas
from temporary sites to permanent accommodations. One of the reasons for the delay is the slow pace of civil
constructions. The Committee found this as an area of great concern. The Committee is at a loss to see that the
construction activities are held up / delayed mainly due to petty administrative and technical reasons. These delays
sometimes run into four to five years resulting in huge time and cost over-run. The Committee hopes that he Department
and the JNV Samiti are alive to this fact. The Committee noted the procedural delay in the communication about
sanctioning of the Vidyalayas is taking in some cases several months. The Committee finds it completely unacceptable. It,
therefore, recommends that henceforth the communication regarding sanctions should be sent to all relevant offices
immediately at various levels, so that the process of preparing plans, drawings, etc. could be commenced instantly.
Action Taken
The delay in shifting of Navodaya Vidyalayas from temporary to permanent accommodation, NVS has initiated
several steps to expedite the completion of Navodaya buildings which are as follows:
-         Allotting construction work to Central / State Government undertaking rather depending upon Government
organization like CPWD / BRTF only.
-         Empanelment of more architects to expedite the process of preparation of plans and drawings.
-         Timely release of funds to Construction Agencies.
-         Regular project review meetings at regional & HQrs level.
            There has been improvement in completion of civil works and shifting of vidyalayas in permanent accommodation
as given below: -
S. No. Year Number of Vidyalayas shifted to permanent building
01. Up to 2001-02 332
02. 2002-03 7
03. 2003-04 13

04. 2004-05 18
05. 2005-06 18

Recommendations/Observations
1.7       The Committee was informed that another reason for delay in completion of works has been lack of proper
coordination between the civil and electrical wings of the CPWD. The Committee had the occasion to interact with the
DG, CPWD who informed that they have now introduced a composite tendering system providing for both civil as well as
electrical works in the same contract, with a view to avoiding these problems. The Committee feels that though the system
of composite tendering system is a welcome development, it would still not rule out completely the possibility of delays
due to other reasons. The Committee feels that in order to see that civil works are not unduly delayed, this activity
including the clearances, etc. from different agencies involved should be completed in a fixed time schedule. The
Committee feels that help of local MP and other representatives of the people can be sought for expediting such clearances
particularly from State Governments and their agencies.
Action Taken
After the assurance given by the DG, CPWD during Parliamentary Committee Meeting, there has been
improvement in this regard. Composite tender for civil as well as electrical works are now being called by CPWD & other
construction agencies.
            Regarding projects delay due to other reasons like land disputes, forest clearance and approach road etc., all
Construction Agencies / Deputy Commissioners of the region have been directed to resolve these issues with the
cooperation of Member of Parliaments and local representatives.
Recommendations/Observations
1.8       The Committee is also of the considered opinion that the tender documents must provide for heavy penalty on the
contractors if they fail to stick to the stipulated time frame fixed for this purpose.
Action Taken
The existing penalty clause has now been modified by the CPWD. As per new clause important milestones for
completion of the projects are to be defined in the tender documents. There is a provision of deduction of 1.5% per month
of delay of tender cost as a penalty in case of non-achievement of each milestone. (Copy enclosed at Annexure-V). The
new clause also provides submission of performance guarantee equivalent to 5% value of the work before signing the
agreement. There is a provision to forfeit the performance guarantee in case of non-performance by the contractor (Copy
enclosed at Annexure-V).
Recommendations/Observations
1.9       The Committee was informed that sometimes the contractors abandon the construction due to unforeseen
developments such as price escalation of iron, cement etc. The Committee is of the view that such cases might be fewer
and far between. The Committee desires that the JNV Samiti and CPWD devise some model and calculate the expected
price rise and time frame to complete the building projects. The construction work should be entrusted to those contractors
who are dependable and have the capability to finish the work.
Action Taken
A price variation clause to compensate abnormal increase / decrease in price of steel / cement has been included in
the tender documents to avoid delay in completion of the projects (Copy enclosed at Annexure-V). All the JNV works are
being executed by Government department / undertakings. These departments have already a system of either registration
or pre-qualification of the contractors so that only financially sound and capable contractors are selected and awarded the
work.
Recommendations/Observations
1.10     The Committee also notes that a lot of time is lost in awarding the works after these are sanctioned. Further, a
change in the plan or site at the last moment also delays the process unduly. The Committee is aware that several

198 th Report on Committe of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/198threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:42:42]
formalities are to be completed before completion / finalization of tender and awarding job to contractors is also a long
process. Yet, the Committee is of the view that it is possible to reduce time in all these to a large extent. The Committee,
therefore, strongly recommends that the entire process from sanctioning the project and awarding the job to the
construction agencies should be streamlined so as to obviate possibility of any delay. Further, on-line tendering may be
tried to cut the delays drastically. There is also need to bring in transparency in the entire procedure.
Action Taken
NVS has now empanelled more architects to expedite  pre-construction activities like site survey, preparation of
drawings and tender schedule. As a result, time required from start of the projects to award of work has reduced from 11-
12 months to 6-7 months.
            All Construction Agencies have been directed to switch over to online tendering system.
Recommendations/Observations
1.11     The Committee has been informed that the Department of Secondary and Higher Education has a Construction
Coordination Committee under the Chairmanship of the Additional Secretary of the Department.  The Committee includes
the Commissioner, Navodaya Vidyalaya Samiti, General Manager (Constn.) in NVS and the senior Managers of the
construction companies.  This Committee meets once in six months to monitor construction of phase-A & phase-B works. 
The Committee is of the considered opinion that the Construction Coordination Committee should meet more often, but
not less than once in two months.  This, the Committee feels, would keep the monitoring officials more attentive and alert
because they will have to report every two months about the progress in construction.  Strict view must be taken in the
cases of undue and unreasonable delays.
Action Taken
            Construction works in JNVs are being executed by CPWD and Central/State undertakings.  These departments also
have their own internal projects monitoring system.  Apart from this Samiti has been conducting quarterly and half yearly
projects review meeting at the regional and Hqrs. level to monitor the progress of the projects.  Samiti has also taken
initiative to develop web based online project monitoring system with the help of National Informatics Centre (NIC).  As
such adequate monitoring system is in place, which is being further strengthened by developing web based monitoring
system.
Recommendations/Observations
1.12     The construction delays in Shillong Region was attributed to the unsettled condition in the North-East.  In fact, the
unsettled condition has also been cited as the main reason for pending civil works in other States like J&K, Bihar and
Jharkhand.  There is no denying the fact that law & order problem also sometimes causes delays in such activities in some
areas.  Surprisingly, the Committee finds that there is no obstruction to railways and other construction works being
carried out at the places like Uri in J&K.  The Committee is of the view that such areas need more quick attention in regard
to schools, etc. than rest of the regions of the country and must be ensured that the law and order aspect may not be taken
as an excuse for delays in construction.  The Committee is of the opinion that the Department should exercise more
caution in choosing the construction agencies for difficult regions.  Engaging local agencies for the construction work may
also be considered.  All out efforts be made with the help of State Governments to ensure that the construction work is
completed well within time.  And if it is unduly delayed, responsibility must be fixed to check any possible carelessness in
this regard.
Action Taken
Samiti has already taken steps to appoint local agencies in North East and Jammu & Kashmir region and other
difficult areas.
All the major works in the J&K region are being executed by JKPCC and JKPWD.  There has been lot of
improvement in completion of the infrastructure in J&K during last two years.  New dormitories, dining hall and
residential quarters have been completed and occupied by the JNV students and staff at Baramulla, Kupwara, Budgam,
Anantnag & Srinagar, etc.  Additional dormitories and residential quarters have also been sanctioned in the J&K region at
various JNVs, which are under full progress.
Similarly, Samiti has allotted works in North East region to local government agencies like Development of
Nagaland Authority (DAN), Meghalaya Government Construction Corporation (MGCC) & Manipur Police Housing 
Corporation (MPHC) & RITES etc. rather depending upon government department like CPWD/BRTF.  As a result during
last two years 12 JNVs have been shifted from temporary site to permanent buildings.  Also additional dormitories and

198 th Report on Committe of HRD
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/198threport.htm[01-07-2016 15:42:42]
staff quarters have been completed in 10 JNVs.
Recommendations/Observations
1.13     The Committee also notes that the land allotted to JNV in Kargil was partially taken over by Defence and it
appears that the Department did not take up the issue with the Ministry of Defence for a long time.  Now that new site has
been identified, the Department must endeavour to complete the required formalities and consultation with district and
defence authorities as soon as possible so that construction work could begin at early date.
Action Taken
The work at JNV, Kargil has already been allotted to the construction agencies like JKPCC and Jammu & Kashmir
Public Works Department. All the drawings and design have been completed and foundation work of various buildings is
in progress.  Construction agencies have informed that working season in the Kargil is limited due to heavy snow fall
during October-March and assured that all the works shall be completed by December, 2008.  Samiti has been closely
monitoring progress of works of the JNV.
Recommendations/Observations
1.14     The Department while explaining the status of construction activities in J&K and Northeast has merely informed
the Committee that the work was in progress in these regions. The `work in progress’ as such does not give a correct status
of work. The Department must in future give the Committee specific stages of the construction so as to enable it to get a
definite view in the matter.
Action Taken
Details status of construction activities in Jammu & Kashmir and North Eastern Region is placed at Annexure-VI,
VII & VIII respectively.
Recommendations/Observations
1.16     The Committee takes note that 30 acres of land is must for opening a JNV. The Committee finds that such a large
piece of land having necessary infrastructure may not be easily available particularly in urban as well as in hilly areas. As
a result, land of this size is allotted, more often than not, in remote areas, which need further time, and more resources to
develop basic infrastructure like approach road, water, electricity, etc. The Committee was informed that land in remote
areas act as disincentive for the contractors who lose interest in these projects resulting in delay and cost over-run.
Action Taken
The Executive Committee in its meeting held on 10
th November 2006 had directed that efforts should be made to
locate the new JNVs close to District HQrs so that all basic facilities like electricity, water, safety & security, approach
roads, support services are easily available and the students do not feel isolated. Samiti has scaled down the requirement of
the land for opening a JNV from 30 to 10-15 acres in case land is allotted near District Headquarters with proper approach
road, water supply and electrical connection etc. However, Samiti would like to inform that in majority of the cases land is
offered at remote locations without any proper infrastructure like approach road, water supply, low lying area etc. by the
State Governments, which not only causes administrative difficulties in running the school but also results in high
development and construction cost.The State Governments are also persuaded to provide better connectivity and urban
feeder power supply to all Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas.
Recommendations/Observations
1.17     The Committee feels that suitable flexibility needs to be brought in the requirement of land for opening of JNVs in
urban, semi-urban and hilly areas. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the State and District Administration
should be sensitized for selecting sites that are suitable, easily accessible and free from encumbrances. After all, the
children of that State are going to be the beneficiaries of these Schools. The Committee at the same time also opines that
the reduced land area should not be a constraint for game and sports activities.
Action Taken
The Samiti has already considered the requirement of land for opening of Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas in urban,
semi-urban and hilly areas including that of North Eastern Region and had decided that 30 acres of land will not be
insisted upon in all the cases. However, in relaxation of the requirement of land has been reduced to 15 to 20 acres in hilly
areas as well as North Eastern Region. Samiti has also decided to agree upon the requirement of land up to 10 acres by
constructing the academic block as well as the hostel in a three-story building keeping in a view that children of that

198 th Report on Committe of HRD

district are going to be beneficiaries of these JNVs. However, the reduction of the requirement of land may not be the
constraint for game and sports activities in the Vidyalaya.
II.        INFRASTRUCTURE
Recommendations/Observations
2.2       The Committee was informed that out of total 498 functional / established Navodaya Vidyalayas, 378 are
functioning at permanent sites in permanent buildings while 120 are functioning in temporary site in temporary  
buildings.   To add to the woes, 36 JNVs out of 378 permanent Vidyalayas do not have a playfield. To this 36 JNVs
another 120 temporary JNVs may be added. Thus a total of 156 JNVs are not having playfield out of the total 498
functional / established Vidyalayas. The Committee finds this situation very disturbing. The Committee is of considered
opinion that the sports help in improving physical & psychological strength of the children and further contribute in
development of overall personality of the children. It is a means of recreation as well. Absence of playfields, therefore, put
them at disadvantage in these regards. The Committee strongly emphasizes the need for making playfield mandatory and
where it is not possible due to small area available, alternate arrangements be made with neighbouring bodies, agencies,
clubs, etc. for allowing students to make use of their facilities.
Action Taken
As on date, 539 Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalaya (JNVs) are functional, out of which, 400 JNVs are functioning at
permanent site. 365 JNVs functioning at permanent site have been provided with proper playfields including 400 meter
track, football / hockey fields, basketball and volleyball courts. Similar playfields are under construction in remaining 35
JNVs functioning at permanent site. Facilities for volleyball, Kho-Kho and Badminton courts etc. are available at 139
JNVs functioning at temporary site also. Construction of Phase-A, which includes construction of playgrounds, for 109
JNVs functioning at temporary sites, is in progress. Efforts are on to provide playgrounds to all schools.

IV.       CRITERIA FOR ADMISSION IN NAVODAYA VIDYALAYAS
Recommendations/Observations
4.1       The Committee notes that the admission to Navodaya Vidyalayas is done on the basis of a Selection Test for
which, certain eligibility conditions have been laid down. The conditions inter alia provide that a candidate appearing for
the Selection Test must be studying in Class-V in a recognized school in that district where he / she is seeking admission.
Admission in Class-VI is given subject to the condition of passing Class-V before admission and also the candidate must
have studied and passed Class III, IV and V from recognized school / schools in the preceding three continuous academic
sessions for which the Selection Test is conducted, spending one full academic session in each class through the formal
system of education, without any repetition of class, gap and / or break in attendance.
Recommendations/Observations
4.2       The Committee notes that unscrupulous people are taking undue advantage of district criterion laid down in the
guidelines. The Committee finds that children of other districts take admission in absentia in Class V in educationally
backward districts where a JNV is situated while continuing their education in reputed schools in urban or semi-urban
areas. At the time of Selection Test, they compete against students of that district who are comparatively weaker, and thus
they have better chance to get admission meant for the rural students of that district. This peculiar aspect has remained
unnoticed and goes against the very basic idea of providing quality education to the rural students of a particular district.
The Committee is of the considered view that the condition of studying and passing Class-III, IV and V in preceding three
continuous sessions needs to be reviewed. The student aspiring for admission in a particular JNV should be asked to
produce a certificate of domicile of that particular district. This would be the most reasonable way to check the influx of
otherwise ineligible candidates.
Recommendations/Observations
4.3       The Committee wants to draw the attention of the Department towards the fact that a large number of poor farmers
and labourers are sending their children to so called `English schools’ running in their villages which are actually local,
private, small-time, non-recognized schools. Also, a good number of children are availing education in informal centres of
learning like EGS & AIE and others being run by the NGOs and supported by the Government. The Committee is not
aware whether children coming out from these non-recognized / informal centres  are eligible to get admission in their
district’s JNV. The Committee desires the Department to reconsider the concept of formal education and see that its aim to
provide quality education to meritorious poor rural students does not get defeated in the cobweb of guidelines which seems
to be a little  away  from  the  ground  reality prevailing in rural areas. The Committee strongly feels that a candidate
coming out of these informal centres or un-recognized school of the village be allowed to take the selection test once he or
she has passed Class-V.
Recommendations/Observations

VII.     PROBLEM OF DROP-OUT
Recommendations/Observations
7.1       The Committee notes that dropout is occurring in different classes of JNVs due to various reasons.  The Committee
finds the vacancies arising due to the drop-out are not being filled up before Class IX   for   the reason that the special
identity of JNVs would not be amenable to newly admitted students as they would not be able to adapt to the new
environment.  The Department has been informed that lateral entry is allowed only in Class IX, which is a stage when the
children are grown up, and special orientation programmes are conducted to bring them at par with regular students.  The
Committee does not agree to this notion of adaptability of students before Class IX.  It feels that the identity of the JNVs
should be made special in the sense that any child who joins the Vidyalaya at any stage must feel at home rather than
experiencing problem of adaptability.  Adaptability for a newcomer is a natural problem.  But the Samiti needs to devise
such teaching methods where the newcomer gets mentally and psychological settled and feels at home at the earliest.
Recommendations/Observations
7.2       Another problem against lateral entry before Class IX as explained by the Department before the Committee was
that holding an entrance test for every class every year is not a viable proposition.  The Committee is of the opinion that
the lateral entry must be allowed to fill up vacancies, if any, in all the classes and not merely in IX and XI classes to ensure
that no seat was allowed to go vacant.  It is a waste of the available resources.  The Committee is not inclined to agree with
the argument of the Department that the number of vacancies being small, it would not be viable to hold an entrance
system for every class every year.  The practice of entrance test is in vogue  in  all  schemes  of  school including private /
public school.  If entrance test could be held every year for VI, IX and XI classes other classes also can be clubbed with
them.  Furthermore, the Committee wishes to reiterate its recommendation about admitting girl students of the area in the
vacant seats.  The Committee desires that no seat be allowed to go vacant when lot of our children remains out of school.
Action Taken
7.1 & 7.2         The recommendations of the Committee have been considered by the Samiti and it has been decided to start

V.        HOSTEL FACILITY
Recommendations/Observations
5.1       Navodaya Vidyalayas being residential schools need to have proper hostel facilities for their students. 
Committee’s attention has been particularly drawn by acute shortage of required staff for efficient running of Navodaya
Vidyalaya hostels.  Committee had accordingly made detailed observations and recommendations in this regard.  The
Committee is, however, disappointed by the follow-up action indicated by the Department.  One striking feature noticed
by the Committee was the acute shortage of Matrons for the Hostels.  One cannot deny the fact that Navodaya Vidyalayas
whether operating from temporary site or permanent site continue to be residential schools and need to have the required
manpower.  Committee’s pointed observation about there being only 36 posts of Matrons filled up against 339 sanctioned
posts has evoked the response that the directions have been noted for compliance. The Committee fails to understand
whether action if any is contemplated by the NVS / Department.  The Committee would like to reiterate that entrusting the
job of supervision of hostels to teachers can be considered only a stopgap arrangement.  Matrons specifically entrusted
with the supervision of hostel facilities to the enrolled students need to be there.  One must not forget that students enrolled
in Navodaya Vidyalayas include both girls and boys coming from different backgrounds and being in formative year of
their lives need to be handled in a professional and efficient manner, which requires 24 hour supervision.  The Committee
had also drawn the attention of the Department towards big gap between the sanctioned and in position status of other
hostel functionaries like Catering Assistant, cook, and storekeeper.  The Committee has been given to understand that
instructions have been issued to all Regional Offices to fill up vacant posts of non-teaching staff.  The Committee strongly
feels that a review of status of manpower available for the hostels of Navodaya Vidyalayas is required to be made on an
urgent basis and make the hostels functional in the real sense by providing the required staff.
Action Taken
It has been decided to provide one post of Matron for looking after girls students in all those Jawahar Navodaya
Vidyalayas where the strength of the girls students exceeds 100. Procedure for appointment of Matron has been simplified
and henceforth the appointment will be made at the school level. To reduce the delay in selection process, the Principal has
already been authorized to renew the contract of the Matron in case her services and performance are found satisfactory.
As on date, out of 366 sanctioned posts of Matron 208 have been filled. Specific directions have also been issued to all the
Regional Offices and Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas to fill up the vacant posts of non-teaching staff by the end of June
2007.
            The status of manpower available for hostels will be reviewed by NVS.
Comments of the Committee
            The Committee is happy to note that out of 366 sanctioned posts of Matron, 208 have been filled.  This can be

            In all JNVs functioning at permanent site, electrical connections from the nearby rural / urban feeder have been

iv)     House system should be strengthened to use it for understanding and significant behaviour changes or deviations,

PREFACE
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource Development,
having been authorized by the Committee, do hereby present this Hundred Ninty-ninth Report of the Committee on North
Eastern Hill University, Shillong.
2.         The Committee had earlier presented its 172
nd Report on University and Higher Education wherein the problems
and challenges before the higher education system in India have been discussed in detail.   This Report, in fact, reflected
the Committee's concern for making our educational system, both world-class as well as accessible.   While holding
consultations for 172 nd Report and also while examining a number of Bills in recent times providing for central
universities in North East, the Committee felt the need for ascertaining the special needs and problems before universities
in this region.
3.         The Committee, accordingly, visited the North Eastern  Hill University, Shillong.  The Committee held extensive
discussion with the Vice-Chancellor, Registrar, teaching faculty, non-teaching staff and the students and attempted to find
the ways and means to help the NEHU become a centre of educational excellence in the country.
4.         The Report was considered and adopted by the Committee at its meeting held on 15
th November, 2007.
NEW DELHI; 
November 15, 2007
Kartika 24, 1929 (Saka)
JANARDAN DWIVEDI
Chairman
Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on  Human Resource Development
           
REPORT
 
            The Committee on HRD being fully conscious of the need and importance of making the higher education
available, accessible and affordable had presented its 172 nd Report on 'University and Higher Education' dealing
comprehensively with almost all the relevant aspects.  This report infact reflected the Committee's strong desire to see the
country become knowledge superpower having a world-class higher education system. It was also conscious of the special
higher education requirements and aspirations of the people of North East. It, therefore, decided to visit the North-Eastern
Hill University, Shillong, one of the greatest and the oldest universities in the region, with a view to have first hand idea
about the existing reality in this regard.
2.         At the Campus of NEHU, the Members of the Committee were received by the Vice-Chancellor, Registrar and
other representatives of the University.  The Committee had a wide-ranging and intense interaction with the Vice-
Chancellor, Registrar, teaching faculty, non-teaching staff and the students.  Several suggestions and proposals were
received for making NEHU a world-class university, with proper infrastructure for teaching and research in various
disciplines including those relevant to local conditions and needs.
3.         The Vice-Chancellor, NEHU, informed the Committee that NEHU was established in 1973 mainly with a view to
pay special attention to the improvement of the social and economic conditions and welfare of the people of the hill areas

199thReport Committee On Human Resourse Development

of north-east region for their intellectual, academic and cultural advancement.  The university with thirty-two academic
departments and five centres of studies had recently been declared as "University with Potential for Excellence" based on
its performance in academics and administration.   He further informed that it ranked among the top nine universities that
had been given this status in the country.  The University had demonstrated that it was fulfilling the objectives for which it
was set up by the Government of India, he said.  The faculty members have received many distinctions by way of awards
and fellowships.  Its students were occupying important positions in the government, private sector and teaching &
research institutions within the country and abroad.  The university has 59 affiliated colleges including minority
educational institutions located in Guwahati (Assam) and Surat (Gujarat).  The Vice-Chancellor informed that the
university had plans to implement complete e-governance and was also committed to provide clean and transparent
administration.
Budgetary Issues
4.         The Registrar of the University presented the physical progress and financial utilization of the grants received by
the university during the Xth Plan period.  He informed that the university had satisfactorily utilized the grants sanctioned
under the non-lapsable pool of the Ministry of DoNER as well as the additional grants provided during the Xth Plan period
for the infrastructure development.   It was also informed that despite the advice of PMO not to impose financial cuts on
the University’s recurring budget as it was located in North-East, it still had to face the financial crunch in the last few
years. 
The Committee has, however, been informed by the Department that there had been no advice to the UGC
regarding financial cuts on the NEHU’s budget.  The UGC releases the funds to the universities out of grants received by
the Ministry of HRD.  Only 5% cut was applied to non-plan expenditure (excluding salaries, pension, interest payments
and repayment of debt) that was mandatory in case of any Ministry and Department.  The Committee is of the opinion that
in view of special requirements of the north-eastern region, even this 5% mandatory cut may be done away with.
5.         The Committee was further informed that the University did not have sufficient funds for repair and maintenance
of its buildings, increasing cost of health care and furnishing of newly constructed buildings, etc.  In the year 2007-08, its
plan funds had been drastically reduced as compared to the previous year.  It was submitted that the university needed
more funds and grant for nurturing and harnessing the true academic potential.  The Department admitted to the
Committee that NEHU deserves much greater financial support from the UGC/Government of India.  However, it denied
that the Plan funds of the university have been reduced over the Plan period or during the current financial year.  The
Department pointed out that against the IXth Plan allocation of Rs.11.34 crores, the original allocation for the university
during the Xth Plan period (2002-2007) was Rs.14.18 crores.  However, with a substantial increase in allocation during the
year 2006-07, the revised Xth Plan allocation stood at Rs.42.52 crores.  For the year 2007-08, i.e. the first year of the XIth
Plan period, an amount of Rs.4147.12 lakh has been earmarked by the UGC for the development of NEHU which
includes: -
i)
                    Development Grant – Rs.2026.32 lakhs.
ii)                   Unspent Balance – Rs.1503.80 lakhs.
iii)                 Revalidation of earlier sanction – Rs.617.00 lakhs.
6.         The Committee appreciates the increase in allocation of funds but it strongly feels that this allocation needs to be
further enhanced substantially to make NEHU a world class institution.   It recommends the Department and the UGC to
favourably consider the budget requirements of NEHU. 
7.         The Committee was informed that NEHU had recently submitted a number of projects for infrastructural
development such as construction of hostels, classrooms, staff quarters, indoor multipurpose gymnasium, etc. particularly
in view of the recently launched Faculty of Engineering and Faculty of Management in the University.  The Department
has suggested that in the XIth Plan the University may take up these proposals with the UGC's XIth Plan Committee.   The
Committee would like the UGC to consider these proposals of the NEHU favourably and sufficient fund may be provided
to the University for these purposes.
Accommodation
8.         Highlighting other problems faced by the NEHU, the Vice-Chancellor informed that despite several new initiatives
taken by the Government to provide infrastructural support, it was still far from adequate.   The academic departments
needed adequate buildings.  The shortage of housing at the campus for all students, teachers and staff was quite acute. 
Students came from far-off and remote places in North East and the university was not able to provide them hostel
facility.  At present it could accommodate only 500 students against the total strength of more than 3500.  The Vice-
Chancellor felt that the university could become academically more vibrant, if hostel facility for all were provided on the
campus itself. 
9.         When the Committee put the problem of shortage of hostels for students and residential quarters for teachers and
staffs before the Department, it replied that the UGC had been providing funds for the construction of Hostels under
General Development Assistance and Special Scheme for Women’s Hostel.  It was submitted before the Committee that

the University may bring the proposals before the XIth Plan.  The Committee, however, was informed neither about the
quantum of funds being provided by the UGC for the purpose nor about the adequacy of the funds released under General
Development Assistance/special scheme for Women’s Hostel to NEHU. The shortage of accommodation was infact,
raised by all sections of the university community who interacted with the Committee mainly on the plea that the forest
and hilly terrain of the area did not allow long distance commuting everyday.   The Committee, therefore, feels that the
shortage of accommodation needs to be tackled on priority basis.  The Committee feels that there was no serious effort
made by the Department or the UGC in this regard.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should
help the University overcome the accommodation problems of its students as well as teaching and non-teaching staff.
Transport facilities
10.       The Committee noted that the university was located far from the city, and a large number of faculty, non-teaching
staff and students had to commute from city to the university campus every day.  The Vice Chancellor informed that there
was hardly any public transport system available and the university's efforts for the last several years requesting the State
Government to ply adequate buses have yielded no results.  On being asked if the Department of Higher Education can
help the university in this regard, the Department submitted that the problem of inadequate public transport system for the
university was primarily a responsibility of the State Government and the university may take up the matter with the State
Government, and the issue, if necessary, will also be followed up by the Central Government.   The Committee feels
concerned to note that the Central Government has not taken this issue as seriously as it deserved.  That City transport in
and around Shillong, is virtually non-existent is known to all of us.  Suggesting to approach the State Government for this
facility, is nothing but passing the buck.  The Committee recommends that to help improve the transport system of the
university, the Department, apart from taking up the matter with the State Government should also ensure that transport
facilities of the University are adequately improved.
New Initiatives
11.       The Vice-Chancellor informed that an important area that was emerging in the region was tourism.  The university
had a proposal to start courses in this field as well.  The Committee learnt that the University had been allowed by the
Department of Tourism, Government of Meghalaya, to set up an Institute of Hotel Management. Indira Gandhi National
Open University and the Indian Council of Social Science Research had also proposed to set up their regional centres on
its land.  The Sports Authority of India has been given permission to set up its Centre with modern sporting facilities in the
University.  The Committee is happy to know that the university was embarking upon newer and relevent areas of study
and was getting favourable help/response from the many agencies such as SAI, IGNOU, ICSSR, State Tourism
Department etc.   For example, the DG, SAI who accompanied the Committee when it visited the SAI Centre being built
in the campus, informed the Committee that encouraged by the university's response, SAI was going to provide more
resources to create world class infrastructure there.   The Committee also after having seen the sprawling and beautiful
campus, is of the opinion that NEHU has the potential for being developed as an important educational-hub of our
country.  The Committee, therefore, calls upon the Department and the UGC to render all necessary help and guidance to
the university in this endeavour.
12.       The Committee was informed that the Honourable Prime Minister had announced the setting up of a College  of
Horticulture/Agriculture and also an Institute of Mass Media at NEHU.  On this issue, the Department clarified that NEHU
had submitted a proposal under Xth Plan for a School of Mass Communication and Information Technology consisting of
a Department of Mass Communication and Information Technology at Tura campus of the University to the then
Department of North Eastern Region (DoNER), Government of India and the University Grants Commission.  While there
has been no response from the DoNER, the proposal was not approved by the UGC during Xth Plan period.  The
Department has suggested that the University might revive the proposal and place the same for consideration by the
UGC’s XIth Plan Committee. The Committee finds that the Department in its reply has chosen to remain silent on the
PM’s announcement about setting up of the two institutes as informed by the Vice Chancellor.  The reason for the DoNER
not responding and for the UGC not accepting the proposals of the NEHU for these institutes, also have not been conveyed
to the Committee.   The Committee only hopes that NEHU would have placed these proposals before the XIth Plan
committee of the UGC that was scheduled to visit the campus.  The Committee would like to have a note on all these
aspects for its consideration. It at the same time calls upon the Departments of Higher Education and DoNER to consider
these proposals favourably.
Issues concerning Non-teaching staff
13.       During its visit the Committee interacted with the non-teaching staff also who submitted a memorandum on their
grievances.  The Non-Teaching Staff Association of NEHU requested for immediate implementation of the proposal of
first financial upgradation to the next higher scale on completion of 8 years of service and for grant of second upgradation
on completion of total 16 years of service in the grade with prospective effect to the eligible group B, C and D grade
employees.  The Committee urges upon the Department/UGC to look into these aspects of staff’s demands/proposals with
the help of NEHU authorities with a view to arrive at a decision in favour of the B, C and D group employees.

Association.  They argued that the manner in which these repatriated staff is accommodated has not only adversely
affected the promotion prospects of the non-teaching staff originally appointed at NEHU but has also resulted in the
decrease in the actual number of sanctioned posts.          In this connection, the Department submitted that when Nagaland
University was established, many regular employees of the erstwhile Nagaland Campus of NEHU opted to join NEHU,
Shillong.  In accordance with the policy decision taken by the UGC/MHRD, 39 such repatriated staff were adjusted in
NEHU against regular vacant posts according to their qualifications.   For the remaining staff, who could not be
accommodated against regular vacancies, their posts were treated as personal to them. Therefore, the contention of the
Non-teaching Staff Association NEHU, that there has been decrease in the number of sanctioned posts is not factually
correct.  According to the University, no non-teaching staff from Mizoram Campus has been adjusted against any regular
post.  The Committee while agreeing with the Department, wishes to emphasise that it should properly address all the
welfare related issues of the staff of NEHU.

16.       There are certain areas where NEHU needs to take sincere initiatives.   The Committee found that there is no
Women Study Centre in the University.  The Committee strongly recommends the University to establish a Women Study
Centre on urgent basis.  Likewise, the Committee also feels that study in emerging areas like bio-technology, nano-
technology as well as traditional knowledge system of North East must be encouraged and pursued more vigorously.
Need for Physical Education
17.       The Committee further noticed that Physical Education had not received the desired importance by the University. 
The University, the Committee feels, needs to give due emphasis to Physical Education.
18.       The Committee also appreciates the role of Department of Higher Education and the UGC in the development of
NEHU.  The Committee finds it worth mentioning that while the existing guidelines laid down by the Department of
Expenditure/Ministry of Finance do not envisage any relaxations for utilization of funds under special conditions like
heavy rainfall & poor construction facilities available, the UGC has extended the time limit of completion of
infrastructural development by two years i.e. March, 2009.  The Committee compliments the Department and the UGC
and expects them to retain their positive outlook and hopes they would do their best to help make NEHU what it deserves
to be - a Center of Educational Excellence in the country.

OVERVIEW 
The National Family Welfare~·Programme was launched in India in 1951, with the 
objective of reducing the birth rate so as to stabilise the population at the level consistent 
with the Nation's !!COnomic growth and development. In spite of this, the alarming growth in 
population is one of the most pressing problems faced by the country, today . . India's 
population, which was 342 million in 1947, has touched 846.3 million according to 1991 
census and has crossed the 880 million mark by the end of 1992. 
India, presently; has about 16 per cent of the world's total population and 2.4 per cent of 
the global land area. The rapid increase in population has serious implications for the overall 
socio-economic development of the Country. Success on -the population front is vital for the 
succe ss of all developmental efforts. . 
The Family Welfare Programme in India is being promoted on voluntary basis. The 
programme seeks to promote responsible parenthood, through independent choice of the 
family planning Method best suited to the acceptor. For conveying the message of small 
family norm to the masses, motivational, educational and persuasive efforts are made 
without any resort to any form of coercion. 
The Family Welfare Programme is being implemented as a centrally . sponsored scheme 
under which cent per cent Central Assistance is provided to the States. Health is a State 
subje ct, but in the case of Family Welfare Programme, the Central Government is providing 
specific guidelines for the successful implementation of the programme.

II 
' METHODS/SCHEMES UNDER THE FAMILY WELFARE PROGRAMME 
TI1e success wheel of family planning programme entirely revolves around the kind of 
methods adopted and the popularity the;;reof. In our country, the procurement and 
distribution of contraceptives is done by the Department of Family Welfare. Under this set 
up, various methods/sei'Vices such as Cu.T., IUD, Oral Contraceptives, etc., are made 
available throughout the country. Amongst the conventional contraceptives, condoms are 
being supplied under free distribution system, through Primary Health Centres, Rural 
Family Welfare Centres and Sub-Centres in rural areas and through hospitals, dispensaries, 
Maternal and Child Health (MCH) Centres and Post Pactum Centres in urban areas. Then 
there is the Social Marketing Scheme providing for sale o( Nirodh at very subsidised rates 
through outlets of various companies. Oral pills were introduced in 1987, facilitating private. 
companies to produce and market the pills. 
Latest techniques include laproseopic sterilisation which calls for supply of United Nations 
Population fund (UNFP A) sponsored laproscopic and Tubal Rings to States/Union 
Territories. For this purpose 20 Central Laproscopic Training Centres have been set up in 
the country to train doctors, nurses and operation theatre technicians. 
During the course of evidence, the Secretary, Department of Family Welfare, informed 
the Committee that sterilisation has become women's programme and as a result 96% of 
sterilisation is performed on women through tubectomy and only 3.5% by vasectomy. 
The Committee feels that this reflected an illconceived bias in the programme and that 
most of the contraceptive methods being popularized are to be used on women and asserted 
that a change in the attitude of planners must be accomplished, so that equal emphasis is 
given on availability of safe methods, both for men and women. 
According to the Secretary, there is relationship between sterilisation and literacy. The 
Secretary confirmed the incidents of death in some cases due to sterilisation but maintained 
that the number of such deaths was declining and a surveillance system was in full swing to 
ensure adequate safety and precautions. 
The Committee regrets the abject mishandling of operation equipment by unqualified 
staff, both in urban as well as in' rural areas. The Committee stresses the need to develop 
infrastructure by starting crash training programmes for all concerned Government or non­
Government persons or bodies to ensure that these methods are administered by properly 
qualified persons only. In addition, the Committee recommends that Government should 
urgently work out a Compensation/Insurance Scheme in cases of deaths due to sterilisation. 
The Committee points out that Government have failed to check the over reporting of the 
sterilisation cases performed by various bodies who haVe been presenting concocted and 
distorted figures. · 
The Committee expresses its deep concern over the abhorrent practice of pre-natal 
diagnostic techniques for determination of the sex of foetus leading to female foeticide 
particularly in urban areas. The Committee feels that such practice has severely affected the 
family welfare programme and is likely to create further imbalance in the male and female 
population ratio. The Committee notes that the Government has already introduced a·draft 
Bill entitled Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (Regulation and Prevention of Misuse) Bill, 
1991 in Lok Sabha and recommends that there should be no delay in passing an effective law 
on this after full discussion. 

The Conutlittee is not Satisfied with the steps taken by Government in so far as the safety 
and testing of contraceptives is concerned. Side effects due to administration of such 
untested contraceptives lead to various ailments and health hazards and jeopardise the 
popularity of the methods. 
The Committee feels that not much research work has been done on development of new 
contraceptives in fndia and the methods introduced by international bodies/companies have 
not proved quite popular. The feedback on the existing contraceptives is also dubious due to 
lack of proper monitoring. 
•· The Committee urges the Government to ensure transparency through proper monitoring 
of quality control and to stop the use of insufficiently tested contraceptives and abortion 
pills. The Committee stresses the need to conduct extensive research in order to upgrade 
condom, safe period techniques, barrier methods and such non interference contraceptive . 
methods, and also to popularise them. 
The Committee recommends that research in the Ayurvedic system of medicine should be 
expanded and strengthened so that indigenously available ingredients may be u~d and 
ancient science revived, for development of alternative contraceptive · methods. 
IMMUNISATION 
The high Infant Mortality rate proved to be a major impediment in the success of the 
Family Planning Programmes in the country. The uncertainty of a child's survival 
necessitated birth of more children in a family. Existence of such tendency among the 
masses called for an effective programme to tackle . this problem. It was in this background 
that the Immunisation Programme was st~rted in the year 1978. This p~ogramme gained 
momentum in 1985 under the Universal I~:Jllunisation Programme (UIP) with the availabil­
ity of additional inputs in all districts in a· phased manner. There are two other centrally 
sponsored schemes which are being implemented to reduce the Infant Mortality Rate-(i) 
OraVRehydration Therapy Programme; and (ii) Prophylaxis Schemes. The rate of ~nfant 
mortality was as high as 110 in 1981. In the last ten years it has come down to 80. 1l1e 
National Health Policy (1983) envisages reduction in the mortality ra~e to below 60 per 
thousand live births by the turn of the century. 
In order to further reduce the infant and maternal mortality rates, UIP PLUS Programme 
named as Child Survival and Safe Motherhood Project was launched during the year 1992-
93; 1l1e project will~ be made operational in· a phased ·· manner. ··"The project is bein~ 
4
· ­
implemented with financial assistance from the World Bank aqd the UNICEF. -, . 
The Committee views the present high rate of infant mortality as a major obstacle to the 
acceptability of small family norms. The Committee feel~ that effective steps should be taken· 
to bring down the infant mortality rate so that people may accept family planning more 
' readily. 
The Committee is not satisfied regarding the full utilisation of the money that is spent on 
the UIP and feels tha~ without participation of · the people at grass root level and 
involvement of institutions like the Pan~hayat, this programme may be lagging behind in 
disadvantaged and backward areas where this is mos~ needed. The discrepancy between the 
performance in one area or one State and another is particularly noted and it is suggested 
that -a more effective monitoring system is required to make up for such discrepancy. 
While welcoming family welfare projects like Child Survival and Safe Mptherhood 
projects, the Committee notes that these are yet to be extended to reach a majority of those 
in dire need of the benefit of these schemes. The relationship of these schemes with the 
Family Planning programme is also yet to be properly explained to the poor urban and rural 
women, who need the advice. · 

TI1e Committee recommends that there has to be a random check on the potency of the 
vaccines and that there has to be better coordination between the Centre and the States for 
the maintenance of the cold chain, so as to retain the potency of the vaccines. 
The Committee also recommends that proper arrangements should be made to ensure 
regular and adequate supply of vaccines . . 

UI 
RURAL HEALTH SERVl~ES 
At present, the rural health infrastructure consists of 20,847 primary health centres (PHC) 
and 1,30,782 sub-centres. The PHC earlier catered to a population of one lakh, now it 
.provides a coverage to every 30,000 rural people, which is further relaxed to 20,000 in tribal 
and other difficult areas. Community Health Centres, with 30 bed rural hospitals and four 
specialists and investigation facilities have also been set up upgrading the PHCs to cover a 
population of 80,000 to 1 ,20,000. · ... 
/ SuB~tENTRES 
Till the end of 7th plan, 1,29,291 sub-ceQtres were functioning and their number rose to 
1 1,30,782 by the end of September, 1992 against the estimated requirement of 1,38 lakh Sub­
centres for the Seventh Plan. Due to non-availability of funds for opening new Sub-centres, 
the targets were not alJQtted to the States/Union territories during the years 1990-91, 1991-
92 and 1992-93. ' 
The Committee notes with concern that while the numerical target in opening Sub-centres 
during 7th Five Year Plan has not been reached, many of those which have been opened are 
suffering from lack of proper maintenance. It also needs proper monitoring as to whether 
sufficient Sub-centres . are being opened in the most needy localities and whether proper 
facilities are being provid ed there. 
The Committee observes that no reasons have been assigned in the Annual Report 1992-
93 for not providing the funds for opening new Sub-centres since 1990, while the World 
B;mk is also assisting in implementation of the Family Welfare Programme. The Comminee, 
therefore, recommends that all the Sub-centres. should be made functional immediately and 
the funds should be provided for opening new Sub-centres . 
TRAINING OF DAIS 
The deliveries in the rural areas are conducted by Dais and they are also involved in the 
propagation of small family norm. 
The Committee is surprised to note that 1.18 lakh untrained Dais are working in the rural 
areas and so far they have not been trained in the profession. The Committee, therefore 
recommends that these Dais should be trained immediately for the improvement of the 
Family Welfare Programme. 
VILLAGE HEALTH GUIDE SCHEME 
The VilJage Health Guide Scheme was started in 1981. To evaluate the working of the 
scheme in various States and Union Territories and to suggest steps required for 
improvement of the scheme, a Task Force was set up in the Ministry in 1989 and its report is 
still under consideration. 
The Committee is constrained to observe that so far the recommendations of the Task 
Force have not been considered and impleme'nted by the Government. Therefore, the 
Committee recommends that a quick decision should be~ taken about implementation of the 
recommendations of the Task Force. The Village Health Guide Scheme should also be 
strengthened so as to achieve the desired objectives. 
'#. 

IV 
ROLE OF INFORMATION AND EDUCATION IN THE 
FAMILY WELFARE PROGRAMMES 
In a vast country like India, where a large number of population is illiterate and poor, it is 
very necessary to create awareness among people about family planning programme. For 
ma~ing it a people's programme in terms of its acceptability 'i.e., popularity, the significance 
of propaganda through information, education and communication is unquestioned. 
The Commiuee has been given to understand that the Government has started a campaign 
through com~n mode of communications like Doordarshan and All . India Radio, in 
addition to printing of posters and advertisements on the merits of family planning. The 
advantages of small family are highlighted through films, plays and spots on Doordarshan 
and AIR and through advertisements for which exclusive responsibility has been entrusted to 
Directorate of Advertisement and Visual Publicity. The Department of Family Welfare is 
giving Rs. 6.5 crores to the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting for exclusive publicity 
on Family Planning matters. 
According to the Government report, in remote and rural areas video vans are sent in 
addition to supply of publicity material or films in the form of audio visuals for making 
people aware of the need for family planning. For this Government have identified 90 poorly 
performing districts in the country. Apart from this Anganwadi Workers, village school 
teachers and educated people in ine rural areas have been involved for spreading the 
message by persuading masses towards small family norms. Active assistance from Mahila 
Swasthya Sangh is also being obtained in the matter. 
/ The Committee views that publicity is an effective way of creating awareness amongst the 
people and feels that proper monitoring and feedback must be provided to publicise various 
family planning schemes. 
As regards publicity campaigns in rural areas the Committee observes that the popularity 
of contraceptives remains confined to the urban and industrial pockets and in rural areas the 
programme is not making any substantial impact due to poor publicity. The Committee 
suggests that the health guides and literate women should be involved at village level for 
convincing rural women about the utility of family planning methods. Voluntary and Non-
Government organisations should be encouraged to undertake the task of publicity. · 
The Committee feels that the present budget provision for publicity of Family Planning 
Programme is not being utilised effectively. In the view of the Committee, it would be better 
if the publicity expenditure is handled by the Department of Family Welfare itself, instead of 
transferring the same to the Information and Broadcasting Ministry and also recommends 
that each Ministry I Department must mobilise its own resources separately by making a 
budget provision for implementation of family planning and Government should accept 
collective responsibility to ensure that burden does not fall on a single Department. 
While inedia publicity is important, if Family Planning is to be made a people's 
programme, it is also important that local grass root institutions like clubs, libraries and 
panchayats should be involved in dissemination of the need for family planning and its 
connection with family welfare. Village and folk art-forms must be used in rural areas. These 
) 
do not require any substantial financial investment, but may be very effective in making the 
people in villages participate in family planning programmes . 
...., 

The Committee observes that the best incentives for family planning are (a) better chances 
f child survival as a result of family welfare services, (b) chances of improvement in 
standard of living and (c) growth of educational facilities. The Committee notes that family 
welfare services and educational facilities have not gone down to the poorest and most 
backward sections of society and this is one of the reasons for sufficient people's initiative 
ot being generated for the Family Planning programme. The Committee recommends co­
rdination among relevant ministries ior this purpose. 
The Committee feels that thorough study should be undertaken of the connections 
tween poverty, illiteracy and fertility rates. The connection between prevalence of child 
~
bour and fertility rates should also be studied. Expansion of family welfare services and 
centives to education, particularly among poverty striken and backward sections is likely to 
scourage child labour and give the people the much needed motivation for Family Planning 
!
rogrammes. Therefore, the Committee recommends the immediate expansion of such 
rogrammes, alongwith proper monitoring so as to ensure that they reach the disadvantaged 
ections both in the urban and rural areas. The Committee expresses its concern over the 
decline of sex ratio from 950 to 927 women per 1000 men. Neglect of the girl-child in 
nutrition and other basic rights has to be remedied at all costs. The lag in education of 
women should also be immediately covered. Laws against child marriage should be made 
more stringent and their proper implementation ensured. 

v 
f ROLE OF VOLUNTARY ORGANISATIONS 
Voluntary Organisations play a vital role in promoting the family Welfare Programmes in 
the country. Their contribution towards making small family norm a people's movement 
needs no emphasis. The complexity and sensitivity of the Family Welfare Programmes, 
which calls for a change in social and personal attitudes, highlights the credibility of 
voluntary workers. 
An amount of Rs. 500 lakhs has been earmarked for the N.G.Os. in the budget estimates 
for the year 1993-94. Financial powers have been delegated to States for approving the 
projects involving N.G.Os. Special schemes have also been evolved for involvement of 
N.G.Os. in the areas which are unserved, under-served or are resistant to acceptance of 
family planning. 
In order to enhance the performance of N.G.Os, Workshops, Seminars and Study tours 
have been organised at State levels. This provides them with an opportunity to interact and 
share experience between the various agencies to monitor the grants. State level SCOV A 
Committees have been set up in some parts of the country to deal with the N.G.O. sector 
schemes and projects. 
With the assistance of United States Agency for International Development, a Private 
Voluntary Organisation for Health (PHOV-II) Scheme has been formulated. The agreement 
envisages provision of fina~cial assistance to the extent of $ 10 million. The voluntary 
organisations are required to contribute 25% of the total cost of project. F0rty such projects 
have been identified for funding and thirty four have been sanctioned. The main objective of 
the project is to reduce morbidity, mortality and fertility among the rural and urban poor. 
The Committee, however, sought further clarifications regarding the USAlD scheme, its 
conditionalities, and the actual manner of involving the NGOs, in the scheme. It was 
emphasized that there must be transparency in the working out of the USAID scheme and, 
on no account, should such schemes become a conduit for experimentations with insuffi­
ciently-tested or possibly hazardous drugs. 
The Committee notes with concern the delay in the sanctioning of funds to N.G.Os in 
some States. The Committee recommends that the flow of funds, equipment and supplies to 
voluntary agencies and organisations should be free and smooth and that the mechanism to 
redress their grievances should be made more accessible to them. 
·The Committee also stresses the need for full and effective monitoring of the work being 
done by NGOs. All schemes involving NGOs must take place under full government 
. supervision. 

VI 
EXTERNAL ASSISTANCE FOR FAMILY WELFARE PROGRAMME 
The internal resource constraint has led the family Welfare Programme in India to go in 
for external assistance. Some projects in the country have been identified and are getting 
.external aid for implementation of the same. The source of such aids are various U.N. 
agencies, Bilateral agreements and International agencies. 
The United Nations Population Fund (UNFP A) has been giving assistance to our country 
since 1974. The major areas where this assistance is . being utilised are for Populatioin 
Education, Area Projects in selected districts., and other such activities. 
Assistance from UNICEF was received during the Seventh Five Year Plan towards the 
Universal Immunisation Programme. During the year 1991-1995, an amount of US$ 107 
million is to be provided by UNICEF for the Child Survival and Safe Motherhood 
Programme. 
The United States Agency for International Development (USAID) is providing assistance 
to-
(a) Family Planning, Communication and Marketing Project; 
(b) Private Voluntary Organisations for Health (PVOH-II Scheme); and 
.(c) Innovations in Family Planning Services Projects in U.P. 
The other bilateral agencies providing assistance for various projects are Norwegian 
Agency for the International D evelopment (NORAD), The Danish International Develop­
ment Agency (DANIDA), Overseas Development Administration (ODA) of U.K. etc. 
The Committee feels that the progress of the projects being run with the help of extemal 
assistance has not been satisfactory. The Committee recommends that the utilisation of the 
external assistance, received and released to the States for implementation of specific 
projects, should be monitored effectively and a study of its impact on the masses be 
undertaken.

VII 
PERFORMANCE 
I 
During the course of evidence, the Secretary, Department of Family Welfare, informed 
that the annual exponential growth rate has risen from 1.25% in 1941-51 to 2.14% in 
1981-91. There has, however, been a slight reduction in growth rate in the last decade. The 
Secretary conceded that the progress has not been as rapid as it should have been. Marked 
variations have also been observed in the success of the programme in various States. The 
States like Goa, Kerala and Tamil Nadu, with crude birth rates of 16.8, 18.1 and 20.7 
respectively, are do·ing very well. On the other hand, the crude birth rates in Assam (30.9), 
Bihar (30.5), Haryana (33.1), Madhya Pradesh (35.8), Rajasthan (34.3) and Uttar Pradesh 
(35.1) are higher than the national average of 29.3 per thousand population in 1991. Similar 
variations are seen in respect of the infant mortality rates. At one end of the spectrum, 
Kerala has an infant mort·ality rate of only 17 per thousand live births whereas it is as high 
as 122 ·in Madhya Pradesh, 126 in Orissa and 93 in Uttar Pradesh. The total fertility rates in 
Bihar (5.1), Haryana (4.4), Madhya Pradesh (4.7) Rajasthan (4.7) and Uttar Pradesh (5.2) 
are significantly higher than the all-India average of 3.9. · 
The Committee expresses deep concern over the slow progress of the programme in 
certain States and recomr:nends that the programme must be implemented effectively 
throughout ~e country. The Government should go into the details of failure of 
programmes in some States to identify the reasons and to take corrective measures. 
The Committee feels that more effective and result oriented measures should be adopted 
to implement this programme of national priority. People must be thoroughly informed and 
convinced about the efficacy of the programme. In order to achieve the desired objective, it 
is imperative to make it a people's programme. 
The Committee finds that some States have not fully spent their funds and feels that · they 
should be more vigilant so that the funds are fully spent and recommends that allocation of 
Central funds to the States should be distributed periodically throughout the year and should 
not be at the fag-end of the year. 
The Committee observes that the statistics given by different bodies, Health Workers and 
I 
even Doctors are being manipulated, thus giving a false and distorted picture of the progress 
of the Family Welfare Programme. 
The Committee feels that proper evaluation of the programme at every level, in all the 
States, be made so that cases of over-reporting may be minimised. This will also help in 
· generating interest and faith in the programme among the masses. 
, The Committee further observes that to make the programme a real success there must be 
j proper monitoring an~ random. checks~ by the aut~orities concerned. Political parties should 
1 also play a constructive role m t~e tmplementatiOn of the programme. : 
I. The Committee expresses its concern over the fact that the Nation al Policy on Population, 
which is before. the National Development Council, has still not been finalised. The 
Committee recommends that this Policy should be formulated without any further delay and 
~ that there should be a national consensus among all political parties on this policy. 

The Committee feels that since Health is a State subject, there must be a coordination 
Committee at the: national level to watch and monitor the Family Welfare Programme from 
the Centre. 
In answer to a question, the Secretary, Department of Family Welfare informed the 
Committee that the Government ·did not at this stage, propose to adopt zero growth rate or 
one-child nonn as targets. The Government wo 'uld think of this only after stabilization of the 
growth has been achievea. For adoption of one-child nonn, infant mortality rate has to come 
down further.

INTRODUCTION
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource Development,
having been authorised by the Committee, present this Two Hundredth Report of the Committee on the Indira Gandhi
National Tribal University Bill, 2007. This Report has the distinction of being the 200
th Report of the Committee that
deals with the Bill providing for the first national tribal university in the country.
 
2.         The Indira Gandhi National Tribal University Bill, 2007 was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 23
rd August,
2007. In pursuance of Rule 270 relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman,
Rajya Sabha, referred the Bill on the 30th August, 2007^^ to the Committee for examination and report.
 
3.         The Committee considered the Bill in its two sittings held on the 30
th October and 15th November, 2007.
 
4.         On the 30
th October, 2007, the Committee heard the Secretary, Department of Higher Education on the Bill. The
Committee in its meeting on the 15th November, 2007 took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill and adopted the
draft report with amendments in clauses 5(xix), 11(3), 23(1), 24(2), 25(2), 26(2), 27, 28 and 39(1) of the main Act.
 
5.         The Committee while considering the report, relied on the following documents:
 
(i)         Background Note on the Bill received from the Department of Higher Education;
(ii)
                Verbatim record of the oral evidence taken on the Bill; and
(iii)               Presentation made and clarification given by the Secretary, Department of Higher Education.
 
6.         On behalf of the Committee, I would like to thank the officials of the Department of Higher Education for
providing necessary inputs and clarifications during the consideration of the Bill.
 
7.         For facility of reference, observations and recommendations of the Committee have been printed in bold letters at
the end of the report.
 
NEW DELHI; 
November 15, 2007

Chairman
