the operation of ICDS projects.  A study covering 150 ICDS projects from all States/UTs and 750
AWCs was carried out by NIPCCD in 2006.  Some of major findings of the survey are as follows:
-
-        Around 59% AWCs studied have no toilet facility.
-        44% AWCs were found to be lacking in (Pre-School Education) PSE kits.
-        36.5% mothers did not report for weighing of new born children.
-        37% Anganwadi workers reported non-availability of materials/aids for Nutrition and Health
Education.
 
The Committee expresses its deep concern over the outcome of this survey.  The Committee
has seen for itself during its visit to AWCs in different parts of the Country- it presents a
dismal picture about the infrastructure and other facilities at AWCs.  Lack of basic facilities,
such as toilets, drinking water, cooking arrangements, etc. reveals the manner in which these
AWCs are functioning.  The Committee feels that lack of adequate and convenient space,
unhygienic conditions, etc. appear to be the main  problems associated with AWCs and once
provision for a building specially designed for the purpose is made it would take care of the
problems mentioned above.  Till the provision for a building for AWCs is made, the
Government should make assiduous efforts for making available basic facilities. Possibility
of utilizing the village schools and community owned buildings for accommodating the
AWCs should also be explored.
 
3.7     Construction of 47,872 AWC Buildings in NE-States was sanctioned as a special case out of the
NER component of the Budget of the Ministry from 2001-02 to 2006-07.  Latest status made
available to the Committee reveals a very unsatisfactory position.  Targets in respect of
construction of AWCs for 2001-02 and 2002-03 have been achieved.   However, there was slow
progress during 2004-05, but during 2005-06 and 2006-07 there has been no progress in the
construction of AWC Buildings. The Committee is aware of the problems/constraints being
faced in the North- East region in construction of AWC buildings due to its peculiar
conditions.  It however, fails to understand the absence of any progress in this regard during
the recent years.  It appears that all activities for this purpose have come to a standstill.  The
Committee was informed that the States were not submitting the UCs of funds released to
them for constructing AWCs.  It appears that they are not able to contribute even 10% of
their share for this purpose.  The Committee is not happy with this state of affairs in the
region, which needs special attention.  It therefore, recommends that it must be taken at the
highest levels to sort out the problems at the earliest, so that the work could proceed at the
desired pace.

5.1     Child Budgeting is an essential tool for monitoring Government’s commitment to the child and the
impact of investments made.  The total magnitude of child specific budget outlays i.e. the total
magnitude of budget outlays on child specific programme/schemes, is referred to as the ‘Child
Budget’.  Child Budgeting has emerged as an analytical tool for assessing the priority accorded to
children in public spending in the country.

VI      THE INTEGRATED CHILD PROTECTION SCHEME (ICPS)
 
6.1     India has a child population of 427 million as per the 2001 census.  The Committee’s attention was
drawn towards the following facts: 
-        India has the largest number of sexually abused children with a child below 16 years raped
every 155
th minute, a child below 10 every 10 th hour and one in every 10 children sexually
abused at any point of time.
-        Number of child labourers increased from 11.28 million in 1991 to 12.59 million in 2001.
-        7981 cases of trafficking and sexual abuse related crimes against children in 2004.
-        0.16 million children in 0-14 years age group are infected with HIV as per the records of
UNAIDS.
-        Number of juveniles increased from 17,203 in 1994 to 30,943 in 2004.  Crimes committed
by them increased from 8561 in 1994 to 19,229 in 2004.
-        11 million children lived on the street in 1997, of which 420,000 lived in the 6 metropolitan
cities.
-        Out of the total number of persons living with disability i.e. 2.19 crore, 35.9% are children
and young adults in the 0-19 age group.  75% of the disabilities are preventable.  Only 1%
of children with disability have access to education.
-        Number of destitute children stands at 44 million.
-        12.44 million children orphans in the country.
 
6.2     The Committee describes the plight of children in our country deplorable.  Their condition
must have worsened further as the last census was conducted in the 2001. The Committee is
of the opinion that the need of the hour is to introspect about our approach, efforts and
resources devoted to overall development of children so far.  The Committee feels that we
have a long way to go  in providing them safe environment free of violence, exploitation,
abuse and neglect so that they grow up into confident and self-respecting individuals.
         
6.3     Integrated Child Protection Scheme (ICPS) is a new centrally sponsored scheme with a view to
create an environment for comprehensive development of children in the country.  The ICPS is
based on the cardinal principle of “protection of child rights” and “best interests of the child”.  The
proposed ICPS was cleared by the Expenditure Finance Committee on 20.3.2008 and is being put
up to the Cabinet for approval.  Plan allocation of Rs.95 crore in 2007-08 remained unspent due to
non-approval of the scheme during the year.  Rs.180 crore has been allocated in 2008-09 for this
scheme.
6.4     Three existing schemes viz (i) Programme for Juvenile Justice, (ii) Shishu Greh Scheme and (iii)

          XI      CENTRAL SOCIAL WELFARE BOARD (CSWB)           
 
11.1   CSWB was set up by a resolution of Government of India in 1953 with the object of promoting
social welfare activities and implementing welfare programmes for women, children and the
handicapped through voluntary organizations.   It was given legal status under Company’s Act. 
The programmes of CSWB are Rajiv Gandhi National Crèche Scheme for the children of
working/ailing mothers, Awareness Generation Programmes, Condensed Courses of education for
Women, Family Counseling Centres, Short Stay Homes for Women and Girls, Working Women’s
Hostel, Mahila Mandals etc.   The Ministry coordinates with the Board on regular basis for
budgetary releases and utilization thereof in respect of the schemes being implemented by the
Board.  There are in all 33 State Social Welfare Boards in States/UTs.
 
11.2   Committee’s attention has been drawn by the under-utilization of funds during the Tenth Plan
Period.  Out of the allocated fund of Rs.170.00 crores for the five years, expenditure incurred was
only Rs.121.20 crore.  The trend of under-utilization of funds continued in the year 2007-08 also. 
Out of the plan allocation of Rs.27.00 crore, expenditure incurred was a mere Rs.2.81 crore upto
31.01.2008.  Even on the non-plan side, out of Rs.12.75crores, expenditure incurred was Rs.6.11
crore only.  The Committee would like to be apprised of the reasons for the underutilization. 
A similar trend of underutilization of funds is being witnessed under Condensed Courses for
Women Education, Short Stay Homes, Awareness Generation Programme etc. 
 
11.3   The Committee has been given to understand that since CSWB is an autonomous body, its
performance has not been evaluated.   The Committee is of the opinion that some sort of
monitoring of the functioning of the Board would be desirable for making its working more

transparent.  It is  responsible for the implementation of so many important
programmes/schemes.  And as can be seen, performance of most of these schemes leaves
much to be desired.
 
11.4   Tendency of having a male child has been common wish amongst the people in the society.
The Committee feels that priority of male child to a female one has led to an imbalanced sex
ratio in the country.  The Committee would like the CSWB to take up in a big way for
spreading awareness in the society about the equal status of female child. The Board would
be doing a better service to the country by carrying forward a dedicated campaign about
importance of female child in the family.  The Committee hopes that the Board would take
up this subject as a mission and come forward with a report on action taken in this regard.  
 
XII    HOSTELS FOR WORKING WOMEN

with day care centre for children is in operation since 1972-73. Under this scheme, financial
assistance is provided to non-governmental organizations, cooperative bodies and other agencies
engaged in the field of women’s social welfare, women’s education etc, public sector
undertakings, women’s development corporation, local bodies, universities, State Governments
etc. for construction of building for Working Women’s Hostel.  This scheme envisages provision

working at places away from their homes-towns, working but husband out of town, widows,

released as on 31.01.2008.

XVIII          NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR WOMEN
 
18.1   The National Commission for Women (NCW) was constituted on 31
st January, 1992 as a statutory
body at the national level, in pursuance of the National Commission for Women Act, 1990 to

XIX   ROLE OF NGOs
 
19.1   Most of the schemes of the Ministry are being implemented through NGOs and their role in
development of women and children is quite important.   Some of the NGOs have done their job
with a missionary zeal.  On a query about monitoring aspect of NGOs, the Secretary clarified that
the Ministry asked the State Governments to furnish the list of NGOs whom grants should be
released.  It is the State Government which monitors the working of NGO.  Central Government
does not have the resources to execute direct monitoring for inquiring about the financial capacity
and the credibility of NGOs and the State Government is relied upon.  However, enquiry is
conducted by Central Government in case of complaint against an NGO.
 
19.2   The Committee appreciates the contribution of NGOs in the field of social and economic
upliftment of women.  Few of them are also doing notable work for development of children.   But
there are complaints or misappropriation of funds, and few NGOs have been blacklisted.   These
blacklisted NGOs sometime manipulate to seek funds and continue draining the nation kitty. Mere
blacklisting will not suffice.  The Committee would like the Ministry to initiate criminal
proceedings against erring NGO as a strong deterrent in the future.  The Ministry should
include the follow up of this recommendation in the Action Taken Replies.
 
XX    CONCLUSION
 
The Committee during the general review of the Schemes implemented by the Ministry has
noted that there has been under utilization of funds in respect of many of the schemes of the
Ministry.  The Committee is aware that most of the Schemes of the Ministry are being
implemented by State Governments and other local agencies including NGOs but this could
not be the only reason.  Under utilization of funds could also be due to many other reasons
ranging from lack of vision, direction and ideas.  Lack of will to execute the Schemes cannot
be ruled out.  The Committee believes that utilization of funds should not necessarily be
wasteful or hurried - it should be spent fairly as well as evenly through out the year with a

that funds are utilized in a proper, smooth and productive manner.  This would also pave

2.8         The Committee expresses its serious concerns over the major gaps between the targets and
the achievements thereof.  The Committee feels that the non-availability of funds is not an issue,
but utilization thereof seems to be the main problem resulting in non-achievement of targets.  
Apparently, there are some serious gaps at each level in the entire delivery system.  The
Committee believes that more impetus needs to be given to all the schemes that concern the most
vulnerable sections of our society i.e. women and children.  Implementing agencies need to be
motivated for more efficacious implementation of the schemes.  Simultaneously, we must have
effective periodical monitoring and review of the performance of the Schemes with a view to
overcome the problems encountered in implementation of these schemes.
 
2.9     The Committee is at a loss to find that UCs remain outstanding from as far back as 1986-87.
It would like the Ministry to continue its concerted efforts to clear pending UCs with active
support from the State Governments. The Ministry has no option but to play a more proactive role
with the co-operation of the State Governments, NGOs and other implementing agencies in
liquidating the pending UCs.   Pendency of UCs  for more than twenty years reflects our
helplessness/ failure in getting these accounts cleared.   The money that is blocked due to this, is a
public money which cannot be allowed to be misappropriated like this. 
 
2.10   The Committee has observed in the past also that it takes normally one to two years to
actually start a scheme, which is a very long time and needs to be narrowed to a large extent.  The
Committee recommends that necessary approvals for the rest of the Schemes should be sought by
the Ministry as early as possible so as to reduce avoidable delays.  The Committee further
recommends that all preparatory exercises including allocation, plan of action etc, of these
schemes should be completed beforehand by the Ministry to ensure their timely implementation.

well as the AWCs sanctioned so far. 
         
3.4     The Committee observes that construction of AWC buildings is the most important
component of infrastructure development so that the services under the scheme could be delivered
efficiently.  The Committee understands that Ministry proposes to provide for construction of
AWC building in XIth plan.  This step, according to the Committee, should have been taken long
time back.  The Committee after having seen during its visits to the AWCs in various parts of the
country, is also convinced that the ICDS Scheme must provide for construction of AWCs for
making it more effective.   The Committee would like the Ministry to explore the possibility of
involving the Ministries of Rural Development, Tribal Affairs, Social Justice and Empowerment
and Health and Family Welfare under their existing Schemes for construction of AWCs.  The
Committee also reiterates its earlier recommendation for fixing a percentage of its allocation for
infrastructure development on the lines of SSA.
3.5     Committee notes that not all AWCs are providing supplementary nutrition. Supplementary
nutrition is, infact, heart and soul of the ICDS Scheme that has to be given to the children and to
the pregnant and lactating mothers.  The Committee views it seriously and it does not know the
reason about this.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to make sure that all the
AWCs must provide supplementary nutrition. 
 
3.6     The Committee expresses its deep concern over the outcome of this survey.  The Committee
has seen for itself during its visit to AWCs in different parts of the Country- it presents a dismal
picture about the infrastructure and other facilities at AWCs.  Lack of basic facilities, such as
toilets, drinking water, cooking arrangements, etc. reveals the manner in which these AWCs are
functioning.  The Committee feels that lack of adequate and convenient space, unhygienic
conditions, etc. appear to be the main  problems associated with AWCs and once provision for a
building specially designed for the purpose is made it would take care of the problems mentioned
above.  Till the provision for a building for AWCs is made, the Government should make
assiduous efforts for making available basic facilities. Possibility of utilizing the village schools and
community owned buildings for accommodating the AWCs should also be explored.
 
3.7     The Committee is aware of the problems/constraints being faced in the North- East region in
construction of AWC buildings due to its peculiar conditions.  It however, fails to understand the
absence of any progress in this regard during the recent years.  It appears that all activities for this
purpose have come to a standstill.  The Committee was informed that the States were not
submitting the UCs of funds released to them for constructing AWCs.  It appears that they are not
able to contribute even 10% of their share for this purpose.  The Committee is not happy with this
state of affairs in the region, which needs special attention.  It therefore, recommends that it must
be taken at the highest levels to sort out the problems at the earliest, so that the work could
proceed at the desired pace.

VI      THE INTEGRATED CHILD PROTECTION SCHEME (ICPS)
         
6.2     The Committee describes the plight of children in our country deplorable.  Their condition
must have worsened further as the last census was conducted in the 2001. The Committee is of the
opinion that the need of the hour is to introspect about our approach, efforts and resources
devoted to overall development of children so far.  The Committee feels that we have a long way to
go  in providing them safe environment free of violence, exploitation, abuse and neglect so that
they grow up into confident and self-respecting individuals.
6.4     The Committee hopes that this revamped centrally sponsored scheme of ICPS would be able
to generate required impetus to our endeavour in providing a safe environment for the holistic
development of children, in need of care and protection.   It expects the Ministry to complete all
the formalities before the implementation of the scheme as early as possible.
 
6.5     The projected outcomes of the Ministry for the year 2008-09 is to mobilize inter- sectoral response
for redressing vulnerabilities and strengthening child protection and setting standards for care and
services of children through Government-civil society partnership.  The Committee hopes that this
umbrella scheme of child protection would be able to address the issues of child protection and
care through three of its schemes to be merged under it from this year.  The Committee would
however like the Ministry to first address all the shortcomings of the three existing schemes to be
merged under ICPS and ensure a regular monitoring of the NGOs and other agencies. The
“National Website on Missing Children” to facilitate training, recovery and rehabilitation of
children who either run away or are missing envisaged under ICPS should also be made functional
as early as possible.
 
6.6     The Committee appreciates the Ministry for providing special shelter care for HIV/AIDS
affected children.  It would advice the Ministry to identify the HIV/AIDS affected children in each
district/State so as to know the number of shelter homes required in each district/State.  The
Committee also would like the Ministry to undertake preparatory exercises for setting up of
Juvenile Justice Boards/Child Welfare Committees and Child Protection Unit in each district.  The
existing Juvenile Children Homes needs improvement and upgradation in the quality of care
provided to children in the institutions, full staff strength, regular and timely release of Central
Grants etc.  The Ministry should focus on these aspects of the existing Juvenile Homes under the
ICPS.

REPORT

1. The Department of Women and Child Development, under the Ministry of Human
Resource Development is engaged in all-round development and welfare of women and
children who constitute roughly two-thirds of the total population of the country.

1.2 The activities of the Department may broadly be classified into three categories—(i)
child-related; (ii) women-related; and (iii) nutrition.

1.3 Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS); Creches/Day Care Centres; Early
Childhood Education, etc. are some of the major programmes being implemented for the
welfare of children.

1.4 As regards women-related activities, the main objective of the Department is to
encourage women to come to the fore and contribute their share to the national
development. The Department undertakes such activities as framing, enactment and
amendment of legislation on women-related issues; formulation of plans, policies and
programmes in the areas of welfare and support services; implementation of employment
and income generation, as well as awareness generation’ programmes; coordination of the
efforts of both governmental and non-governmental organisations engaged in the field of
women and child development, etc. To make women self-reliant by enhancing their
employment avenues, training is being imparted to them in conventional sectors like
agriculture, dairying, handicrafts, sericulture, fishries, etc. and also in modern vocations such
as electronics, computers, beauty culture, catering, etc.

1.5 Two schemes namely, Rashtriya Mahila Kosh and Mahila Samridhi Yojana have
also been launched in recent years to take care of the credit and marketing needs of the self
employed-women as well as women engaged in the informal sector. Side by side, in order to
provide safe and cheaper accommodation to single women working in cities/towns, the
scheme of hostels for working women, and creches/day care centres to ease out the child
care burden of working mothers are also being supported by the Department.

1.6 The Department, through its different schemes, is not only trying to provide
pregnant women, nursing mothers, as well as children, with nutritious food but also making
them aware of its necessity. Nutrition Education & Extensions; Itegrated Education in
Nutrition; quality control laboratories; production of nutritious foods through NGOs with
UNICEF assistance etc. are some of the schemes being implemented in this regard.

1.7 However, all these efforts and initiatives have not been able to bring about the
desired level of improvement in the condition of women and children. A large number of
women, particularly in the rural and backward areas, continue to be the victims of age old
social evils and are economically dependent on men. In the urban areas, particularly in the
metropolitan cities, cases of atrocities against women and their exploitation are on the
increase. The condition of children is not better either and is marked by such disconcerting
features as high incidence of malnutrition, abnormal rate of infant mortaility, female
foeticide; prevalence of common disorders like Vitamin ‘A’ deficiéncy, iodine deficiency in
some areas; extremely low levels of opportunities for early childhood stimulation, etc.

2..The Committee notes that the budgetary allocation, both plan and non-plan, to the
Department of Women and Child Development this year is Rs. 730 crores and Rs. 44.89


crores respectively. This amount, the Committee notes, is higher only by Rs. 69.3 crores as
compared to the B.E. of 1994-95. During the course of her oral evidence, the Secretary,
Department of Women & Child Development, admitted that the amount provided this year
would be inadequate and that the Department was given Rs. 730.00 crores in the Plan
against a demand of Rs. 965.00 crores.

2.1 The Committee is of the opinion that some of the important and useful schemes
relating to women and child development have remained non-expanding mainly due to
resource constraints inspite of the fact that there are no other schemes adequate to
supplement or replace these schemes and which need to be strengthened. The Committee
feels that the Planning Commission, by providing much less than what was asked for, has
not taken a realistic view of the requirements of the Department.

2.2 In view of the price escalation and other related factors, this increase, would not be
enough to sustain even the on-going projects. While the women and child shouid have
received the utmost consideration of the Government, only 4.28% of the total budget of the
Government has been earmarked for their welfare. Children and women being the most
vulnerable sections, a developing society like India’s can ill-afford any slackness at this
juncture in the implementation cf schemes meant for their development.

2.3 The Committee, therefore, recommends that adequate provision should be made to
the Department so that it may not only continue its ongoing projects but also expand and
strengthen many of its important schemes.

2.4 The Committee, however, finds that there is a big gap between the amount spent so
far on various schemes like creches/day care centres, training of ICDS functionaries,
Balwadi Nutrition Programme etc. and that provided for the entire 8th Plan period.

2.5 The secretary explained that the slow progress in appropriating the 8th Plan outlay
in the case of certain programmes, in fact, was mainly due to the non release of
proportionate amounts every year by the Planning Commission. She, however, maintained
that such was not the case with all the schemes and, in fact, the 8th Plan outlay would fall
short of the total requirement of the Department.

2.6 The Committee is constrained to observe that the progress of expenditure in case of
the schemes mentioned above is not satisfactory and hence their implementation is tardy. It
fails to understand as to"how the Department would appropriate the surplus provision in
regard to those programmes within the remaining one year of the 8th Five Year Plan. The
Committee feels that either the overall performance of Department was not found upto the
mark by the Planning Commission er the Department was not able to convince the Planning
Commission about its requirement. The Committee recommends that the Department should
plead its case strongly before the Planning Commission to get maximum funds released at
the RE stage this year and also in the terminal year of the plan.

2.7 The Committee notes with great concern that there appears to be a tendency in the
Department to proliferate more and more schemes having identical activities. Such a
fragmented and unorganised approach results in wastage of scarce resources. For example,
for imparting vocational training to women, the Department has such schemes as (i)
Condensed Courses for Education for Adult Women and Vocational Training; (ii) Support
to Training and Employment Programme to Women; (iii) Training and Employment-cum-
Production Centres for Women; (iv) Assistance to Voluntary Agencies for replication of
successful Programmes; and (v) Integrated project for Development of Women. Similarly,
Indira Mahila Yojana. Rashtriya Mahila Kosh, Mahila Samridhi Yojana and other socio-
economic programmes also appear to have a common objectives and overlapping activities.



Likewise, Information and Mass Education Cell; Integrated Nutrition Education; Nutrition
Education and Extension, Mass Media Communication are engaged in spreading
information/awareness about nutrition.

2.8 This fact was pointed out by the Committee in its 7th Report (para 44) also, but
no satisfactory reply has been given by the Department in its Action Taken Report.
Therefore, the Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation and urges upon the
Department to revamp and rationalise all such schemes. It also suggests that instead of
allocating a token amount for all of them every year, the Department should concentrate
on and consolidate only important and meaningful schemes.

Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS)

3. The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) aims at providing an integrated
package of services to children below the age of six years, pregnant women and nursing
mothers. It is one of the major components of the Department which alone accounts for
approximately 65% of the total budgetary allocation.

3.1 The Committee notes that Rs. 512 crores has been provided for this scheme in
1995-96, as: against Rs. 434 crores last year. The Committee was informed that this
increase was mainly for expanding the programme by sanctioning. new ICDS projects in
uncovered blocks/urban slums and for sanctioning Indira Mahila Yojana (IMY) in 200
blocks, for which an amount of Rs. 12 crores is also included in it. On being asked, it was
stated by the Secretary that the amount provisioned for ICDS scheme this year would be
sufficient not only for meeting the operational costs of existing projects, but also for taking
up the proposed 463 new projects, presently under the consideration of the Planning
Commission.

3.2 The Committee was also informed that out of 3774 ICDS Projects sanctioned upto
December, 1994, 3342 have been made operational so far. The proposal of the Department
for the universalisation of ICDS scheme during the remaining period of the Eighth Five
Year Plan has been submitted to the Planning Commission and is awaiting its approval.

3.3 The Committee is not satisfied with the progress of this scheme, as even after 25
years of its operation, the ICDS projects could not be provided in all the blocks of the
country. The target of universalisation of this scheme during the Eighth Five Year Plan
appears to be a far cry. The Committee is anguished to note that the proposal for
universalisation of ICDS scheme has been pending with the Planning Commission for a
long time. The Committee is constrained to observe that there appears to be slackness on
part of both, the Department as well as the Planning Commission in finalising the
proposal.

3.4 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should pursue the
pending proposal vigorously with the Planning Commission and get it cleared without any
further delay.

3.5 The outlay for the ICDS scheme provided this year which also includes a
component of Rs. 12 crores for the Indira Mahila Yojana does not appear to be adequate.
It is not commensurate with the goals that the Department has proposed to achieve. The
Committee is unable to understand as to how the Department would be able to meet the
expenditure for taking up so many new ICDS projects in 1995-96 as well as bearing the
operational costs of the existing ones. The Committee therefore, suggests that the Planning
Commission should make a realistic assessment of the financial requirements for achieving
universalisation of ICDS Scheme and provide a suitable amount for this purpose.

3.6 The Secretary, Department of Women and Child Development, stated that an
ICDS project took 18 months to be fully operational. The Committee feels that the time


taken in this regard is long and the Department should make efforts to minimise it to the
extent possible.

3.7 The Committee observes that, over the years, more and more new schemes/
components have been added to the ICDS scheme, such as Creches; Adolescent Girls
Scheme; Early Childhood Education and Indira Mahila Yojana . Besides, Anganwadi
workers are also in great demand in implementing such programmes as family planning,
National Literacy Mission, etc. The Committee apprehends that the overburdening of this
scheme might lead to the deviation of the scheme from its main objective and over-streching
of financial allocations.

3.8 Despite the integration of so many schemes into the ICDS in due course, the staff
strength of its centres remains the same, as originally (5 vided. The Committee suggests that
a study should be cenducted to find out whether th. staff strength of the ICDS centres in
the present circumstances is sufficient or not. As regards addition of new components to it,
the Committee recommends that this matter be given a fresh look by the Department. While
the Committee has no objection for taking up additional components, it recommends that
adequate and separate allocation be earmarked for all the additional components so that no
funds need be diverted from the main ICDS scheme.

3.9 The Committee is surprised to note that while the Department has shown to have
achieved the target of opening new ICDS projects and also of utilising the given funds, there
is a shortfall in achieving the target of beneficiaries for the last three years. The Department
informed that this shortfall was owing to under-reporting of ICDS projects. The Committee
feels that the Department should be more vigilant in this regard and should see that this sort
of under reporting is avoided.

Training of ICDS Functionnaires

4. A comprehensive training programme for the ICDS functionaries at various levels, is
being run by the Department with the help of the National Institute of Public Cooperation
and Development (NIPCCD), voluntary organisations, State Governments and Uttar
Pradesh Bharat Scouts and Guides. At present, There are 304 training centres for various
levels of programme functionnaires. a

4.1 The Committee notes that the target of imparting training to the ICDS functionaries
has remained static for the last three years and is not commensurate with the increase in the
ICDS projects over the years as shown in the table below:

Year छा No. of Projects Increase
1992 (upto 31.12.92) 2765 _
1993 (upto 30.9.93) 2871 - 106
1994 (upto 30.9.94) 3187 316
: As on 31.3.95 3899 712

4.2 The Committee feels that, with the present rate of increase in the number of
projects, the requirement of trained functionaries is bound to grow. It recommends,
therefore, that a thorough assessment of the requirement of trained functionaries may be
undertaken and the target of imparting training to the ICDS functionaries should be
accordingly revised.

4.3 It is also. noted that there was shortfall in achieving the targets set for training the


ICDS functionaries at all levels during the year 1994-95. Non-deputation of trainees by the
State Governments and non-reporting of trainees at training centres were the reasons given
by the Department for this shortfall. On being asked as to why the State Governments are
not deputing trainees and why those who have been deputed are not reporting, the Secretary
stated that it was mainly because of slow pace of recruitment and some court cases. The
Committee expresses it concern over this phenomenon as it would adversely affect the
progress of the ICDS in the long run and recommends that the Department should make all-
out efforts to sort out this problem with the State Governments immediately.

World Bank Assisted ICDS Projects

5. At present, there are two World Bank assisted ICDS projects, ICDS-I for Andhra
Pradesh and Orissa; and ICDS-II for Bihar and Madhya Pradesh. These projects, apart from
the package of services envisaged under the ICDS schemes, also include such components as
income generating activities for women, construction of Anganwadi buildings, Nutritional
Rehabilitation Centres, etc. The period of ICDS-I project is 1990-91 to 1995-96 while that of
ICDS-II is 1993-94 to 1999-2000 A:D.

5.1 The total Eighth Plan outlay under the World Bank assisted ICDS is Rs. 330.00
crores, whereas the Department has been able to make use of only Rs. 240.42 crores so far.
Even in the penultimate year of the Eighth Five Year Plan, the budgetary provision
earmarked is only Rs. 64.00 crores. In this way, a hefty amount of Rs. 90.00 crores remains
unutilised.

5.2 On being asked as to whether the Department would be able to fully use the
unutilised amount, the Secretary explained that since the ICDS-II was gaining momentum,
more resources would be required and, therefore, the Department was hopeful of utilising
the available amount during the Eighth Five Year Plan. The Committee recommends that
the Department should ensure that the available resources be utilised in right earnest and
there should not be any let up in this regard.

5.3 As regards the ICDS projects, started with World Bank Assistance, nothing is
known about their fate after the flow of funds ceases on completion of the stipulated period
because no separate provision for it has been made. The Committee suggests that the
Department should continue with those projects by providing adequate allocation etc.

Creches/Day Care Centres/National Creche Fund

6. The scheme of Creches/Day Care Centres was started in 1975. It was proposed to
start 50,000 additional creche units during the Eighth five Year Plan at the rate of 10,000
every year. But there has not been any increase in the number of creches since 1991-92. The
sole reason for this was stated to be inadequate resources. The Committee, however, notes
from the table, showing financial targets and achievements, that the Department has not
been able to achieve the financial targets during the last three years owing to some reason or
‘the other. The Committee is baffled to learn that while the Department was not able to
open any creche since 1991-92, due to alleged inadequate funds on the one hand, it was not
able to achieve its financial target during the last three years on the other.

6.1 Now that more and more women are coming out of their hearth and opting for
newer vocations, requirement of creches is being felt in smaller cities and towns also. The
Committee feels that since the National Creche Fund has been established, the Department
should make all out efforts to meet the requirement of creches all over the country through
this scheme.

6.2 The Department has in. its note’ supplied to the Committee, mentioned that
consequent upon audit report and CBI inquiry, 25 creches run by the Indian Council for


Child Welfare, and 6 run by the Bhartiya Adim Jati Sevak Sangh had been closed
temporarily Fifty creches run by the Central Social Welfare Board have been cancelled and
sanction of 68 creches run by the Bhagini Nivedita Pratishthan, Karnataka, has been
withheld pending an enquiry.

6.3 On being asked as to how fake and bogus organisations managed to receive
Government grants and whether their antecedents were thoroughly checked before funds
were sanctioned to them and what mechanism the Department had to keep a check on this,
the Secretary, Department of Women and Child Development replied that whenever
irregularities came to their notice, either through a complaint made or during our regular
inspection, necessary action was taken. The Committee is thus given to understand that the
Department does not have any effective mechanism of supervision and monitoring and it
relies mostly on the complaints which are brought to its notice. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that a foolproof system of supervision and monitoring (including proper
auditing) to ensure proper utilisation of funds be evolved. It also recommends that the
organisations, found to be involved in committing irregularities and misuse of funds, be
blacklisted and debarred from receiving any sort of grant under any scheme of the
Department. A list of such organisations may be circulated to all other Ministries/
Departments. The Committee also suggests that the Department should undertake random
checking frequently.

6.4 The amount, which remains unspent owing to closure/cancellation of certain creche
centres involved in irregularities , should not be surrendered by the Department; rather it
should be used, for opening new creches wherever necessary.

6.5 The Committee expresses its dissatisfaction over the progress of the action taken in
pursuance of its recommendation made in its two previous reports (3rd and 7th) on the need
to conduct an enquiry into the affairs of the Bhartiya Adim Jati Sevak Sangh, which has not
been completed even after almost one and half years. The Committee desires that the matter
be .expedited.

6.6 Malpractices and irregularities on a large scale, the Committee feels, put a question
mark on the credibility of volunatary organisations like Bhartiya Adim Jati Sewak Sangh
(BAJSS). The Committee is also not happy with the working of organisations like the
Central Social Welfare Board and ICCW, which are receiving huge amount of grants from
the Department.. The Committee is constrained to observe that the Department has failed in
its task of ensuring proper utilisation of the hefty sums being given to them. While
appreciating the attemps of the CSWB in the areas where ICDS projects have not been
provided, the Committee is constrained to express its unhappiness over the general working
of the Board where a major chunk of the grant is being spent on administration and very
little on other activities. The Committee reiterates its earlier suggestion to assess the
functioning of the CSWB without any delay so as to remove all lacunae in its working.

Early Childhood Education Scheme

7. This scheme is being implementea through voluntary organisations in nine most
educationally backward districts of the country, the major beneficiaries of which are the
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

7.1 The Committee is quite unhappy to note that this programme has remained static
since 1988 due to financial constraints and this year also, budgetary provision under this
scheme is the same as that of last year.

7.2 The Committee finds that it is a very good scheme meant for preparing children for
entry into primary school by taking care of their social, mental, physical, moral and


emotional develapment. But the chances of its expansion appear to be very bleak with the
present level of allocations. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government
should provide sufficient funds for this scheme so that it'could be extended to more and
more districts having large SC/ST population.

7.3 The Committee feels that the rate of honorarium to teachers and helpers is nominal
considering the escalation of prices. The Committee, therefore, suggests that the rate of
honorarium be appropriately enhanced.

Child Prostitution

8. The Committee feels strongly about the prevailing practice of child prostitution in
India. The Committee was informed that a proposal had been moved in pursuance of the
directive of the Supreme Court for strengthening the implementation machinery for
coordinated efforts ut national and State level, to combat the evil of child prostitution and
also to rehabilitate prostitutes/devadasis. A proposal to set up a Special Cell for this purpose
has also been moved.

8.1 Though the Committee is happy that some steps for strengthening the
implementation machinery have been initiated by the Department, it feels that simple
strengthening of the existing machinery would not be enough. The Committee is of the
opinion that the problem of child prostitution has not received due attention so far and
emphasis has been more on legal than developmental or rehabilitative aspect of this
problem. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a multi-pronged strategy be evolved
for combating this evil effectively. It also recommends that the proposal of the Department
to set up Special Cells for this purpose be cleared at the earliest.

Cultural Exchange Programme

9. The Committee notes that this scheme has virtually remained on paper for the last
five years and every year a token allocation ranging from Rs. 50,000 to Rs. one lakh is being
made. Asked about this, the Secretary stated that it was being kept alive in the hope that
some proposal might be received in future. The Committee is of the opinion that since a
number of good scheme are facing financial constraints, there is no point in blocking money
for this scheme which may better be wound up.

Indira Mahila Yojana

10. The Government has been reiterating its commitment about implementing the Indira
Mahila Yojana for the last several years but it is yet to take a final shape. This scheme has
nothing new to offer to women, since the awareness generation and income generation
components are already being taken care of by various other schemes of the Department. Its
novelty lies, to some extent, in offering an integrated delivery of services to women as
against the previous fragmented systems on which the Committee in its earlier report (7th
para 21), has commented: “whether a single-window delivery system would benefit women
in immensely varied circumstances has also to be assessed .”

10.1 In this background, the Committee is of the view that instead of intermingling it
with ICDS, the awareness generation components of the Indira Mahila Yojana should be
taken up as a new scheme and the other schemes of awareness generation should be merged
with it. The Committee is happy to learn that the Department has already submitted a
detailed proposal on this to the Planning Commission. The Committee suggests that the
Department should make efforts to get the said proposal cleared as early as possible.

Mahila Samridhi Yojana
11. This scheme aims at encouraging the saving habit among rural women and is being


implemented through a network of 1.30 lakh post offices in the rural areas. Under this
scheme, a total of 80.47 lakh accounts have been opened, with a deposit of Rs. 77.85 crores
by the end of February 1995.

11.1 The Committee was informed that an increase to the tune of Rs. 10 crore in the
budgetary provision in 1995-96 had been made, mainly to pay the incentive to account
holders, and also to pay operational cost to the Deptt. of Posts.

11.2 The Committee notes that the target of opening 1.50 crore accounts under this
scheme could not be reached last year. The Department has, in its note furnished to the
Committee, pointed out, inter alia, that the Department of Posts could not provide adequate
number of Staff and stationery in the rural post offices for the purpose. It has also been
brought to the notice of the Committee that smaller amounts generally are not accepted by
the Post Offices. The Committee suggests that the Department should take up the matter
with the Deptt. of Posts and ensure speedy and effective implementation of this scheme.

11.3 In response to the Committee’s recommendation, made last year, to extend this
scheme to the urban areas also, the Secretary informed that the planning Commission has
decided to take this matter into consideration only after two years of its implementation.
The Committee fails to understand as to why the Planning Commission has lacked to wait
for two yeurs, while the scheme has proved to be useful in the rural areas. The Committee,
therfore recommends that the matter may again be taken up with the Planning Commission
so that the scheme may be extended to the urban areas, with suitable modifications.

11.4 The Committee expresses its unhappiness over the poor response to the scheme in
States like Bihar (12%), Gujarat (20%), Maharashtra (31%), Rajasthan (15%) and West
Bengal (11%). The Secretary clarified that the Department was taking up this matter with
the State Governments because it was mainly they who were responsible for implementing
the scheme. The Committee recommends that the Department should intensify its efforts to
enlist the requisite cooperation from the State Governments. The Committee also suggests
that the Department of Posts should be requested to provide adequate number of Post
Offices in tribal and rural areas so that more and more women could be benefited by the
heme. The Committee emphasises the need for making adequate publicity about the
scheme through mass media. The Committee feels that elected local bodies could play a
significant role in this regard and hence suggests that their help may be taken by evolving a
suitable mechanism. The cooperation of Mahila Mandals and other NGOs may also be
enlisted.

Working Women’s Hostels

12. The financial allocation under this. scheme for this year in the same as that of last
year i.e. Rs. 7.75 crores, inspite of the fact that evaluation studies undertaken by the
external agencies have underlined an emergent need to expand this programme and to
upgrade the facilities in the hostels. The committee, in its previous report, while expressing
concern over the inadequacy of hostels for working women, had recommended that
construction of more hostels should be encouraged. This has become more necessary in view
of the fact that the progress of the scheme during the years 1992-93 and 1993-94 was very
poor. Last year also, the Department had to reduce its original target of constructing 60
hostels to 50 in view of the cost escalation factor. Keeping the budgetary allocation at the
last year’s level shows that the Department has not taken the recommendations of the
Committee seriously. The Committee however, reiterates that the allocation for this scheme
be adequately enhanced so that the backlog of the last three years could be cleared. It



7

should also, at the same time, encourage more and more voluntary organisations to come
forward in this field by increasing their grants.

12.1 In reply to the Committee’s recommendations made last year for evolving a system
of monitoring to contain cases of irregularities and mismanagement of the hostels, the
Department has stated that the existing system in this regard was adequate. But the
Committee is not convinced by the reply given by the Department, as more and more cases
of irregularities and atrocities committed against the inmates are being reported. The
Committee therefore reaffirms its previous recommendation of including one government
representative on the Board of Management of each of these hostels.

Atrocities Against Women

13. The subject of initiating legal action in cases of atrocities against women falls within
the purview of the Ministry of Home Affairs. The Committee, however, feels that the
Department of Women & Child Development, being the nodal agency to look after the
welfare of women, should work in close tandem with the Ministry of Home Affairs in this
regard. It becomes all the more necessary in view of the fact that incidents of atrocities
against women are increasing day by day. It is a matter of concern that “Crime against
Women Cells” have been set up, so far, only in 12 States/UTs. Therefore, the Committee
recommends that the Department should take up this matter with the Home Ministry and
see that such Cells are set up in the remaining States/UTs at the earliest. It also sugges*s
that studies on the subject of violence against women, initiated by the Department, anc the
Bill on “Domestic Violence against Women.” which is presently under consideration should
be expedited so that follow up action could be taken without much delay.

13.1 The Committee suggests that the Legal Literacy Manuals, prepared to create
awareness among women about the laws concerning them, should be made available in
regional languages as well.

13.2 The scheme of “Education Work for Prevention of Atrocities against Women”, it
appears, has not made much headway. The allocation for this purpose has remained static
for the last two years. The amount of Rs. 35 lakhs, provided for this scheme in 1995-96,
does not inspire enough hope. There is a greater need for intensifying the educational
publicity against atrocities on women. The Committee, therefore, recommends that sufficient
provision be made for this important programme. The Committee also suggests that a
separate fund be created in the Department for rehabilitating the victims of atrocities,
particularly the young girls.

Rashtriya Mahila Kosh (RMK)

14. The Committee noted that the Rashtriya Mahila Kosh (RMK) has sanctioned credit
limit to 48 NGOs to cover 62,322 women in the first two years, as against the target of
covering two lakh women in a six-year period. It is also noted that its performance in terms
of disbursement has been poor. The main reason for low disbursement, the Department
stated, was low consumption capacity of poor women who were the target beneficiaries. The
Department expects greater demand for loans this year. The Committee feels that lack of
awareness about this scheme in the rural and far-flung areas is also one of the major reasons
for low disbursement. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should
take necessary steps to give wide publicity to the scheme. As the scheme is being
implemented. mainly through Voluntary Organisations, it also recommends that the
Department should ensure that only those organisations which have good credentials are
involved in this scheme.


National Commission for Women (NCW)

15. The Committee expresses its concern over the ‘ela’ in reconstituting the
Commissions. Although its term has expired quite some time back. It is also unhappy to
note that the Annual Reports of the financial Commission for Women have not been placed
so far before the Parliament. The Committee hopes that the Commission would be
reconstituted soon and its Annual Reports presented to the Parliament regularly.

Support to Training and Employment Programme

16. Under the scheme of ‘Support to Training and Employment Programme for
Women’, projects are sanctioned for income generating activities and support services on
90:10% cost sharing basis.

16.1 The Committee was apprised that at present, 25 projects were at various stages of
implementation and that the budget provisions were fully utilised during the last three years
for operating the ongoing projects, besides sanctioning some new projects every year.

16.2 The Committee is of the opinion that this is a good scheme which is gathering
momentum. In view of this, more proposals from unrepresented areas/sectors also are likely
to be received. It would give rise to more demand for assistance under the Scheme. ‘The
Committee feels that the provision of Rs. 16 crores for 1995-96, would not be sufficient to
meet the requirements of both ongoing projects, as well as extending the scheme to new
areas/sectors. The committee, therefore, recommends that more funds should be provided
for this scheme. To make the Scheme more attractive, the Department, the Committee
feels, should devise method for helping the trainees in taking a suitable occupation/
employment.

Women’s Bureau

17. The Committee was informed that there had been tremendous increase in the work-
load of the Women’s Bureau due to setting up of National Commission for Women,
Rashtriya Mahila Kosh, etc. The sanctioned strength of the Bureau continues to be almost
the same as was approved in 1976. A proposal to create a division in the Bureau, the
Committee was informed, is under consideration and the Planning Commission has agreed to
provide the necessary funds for the proposal. In view of the important responsibilities and
increasing work-load of the Women’s Bureau, the need for increasing its staff adequately,
the Committee feels, is quite genuine. It, therefore, recommends that this mater.should be ©
taken up with all concerned and the needful be done urgently.

Family Counselling Centres

18. The programme of Voluntary Action Bureaux and Family Counsalling Centres was
launched by the Central Social Welfare Board in 1982 with a view to extending preventive,
curative and rehabilitative services to those women and children who are the victims of
atrocities and exploitation.

18.1 An evaluation of these family counselling centres undertaken by the Government
of India through National Institute of Public Cooperation and Child Development
(HIPCCD) had highlighted inter alia the need to strengthen its infrastructure. The
Committee is also given to understand that grants for some of the centres had not been
released last year. . E

18.2 The Committee is surprised to note that inspite of the above position, a drastic cut
has been made this year in the allocation for this scheme it has been reduced to Rs. 1 lakh
this year as against Rs. 2.00 crores last year.

18.3 Questioned whether the Department wants to continue with the programme, the
Secretary said that the Central Social Welfare Board had substantial budget for family


counselling centres. But this does not hold good in the face of the allocation made this year.
The Committee, therefore, feels that this important scheme should not be starved of funds.
It also recommends that the outstanding dues of the centres be released forthwith.

National Nutrition Policy

19. The National Nutrition Policy (NNP) aims at tackling the problem of malnutrition in
the country through a set of various direct nutrition interventions of vulnerable groups and
indirect policy instruments involving long term institutional and structural changes.

19.1 The Committee was informed that as a follow-up of the NNP, a Nutritional
Surveillance System is being developed and District Diet and Nutrition Profiles are being
prepared for identifying area specific deficiencies and strategies to combat them are being
worked out.

19.2 The Committee is happy that the National Nutrition Council set up as an apex
body to oversea and monitor the implementation of NNP, is headed by the Prime Minister
himself. The Committee emphasises the need for having such bodies at the State level
headed by the respective Chief Ministers. It also suggests setting up ‘of inter-departmental
coordination Committees in all the States for monitoring the implementation of the policy.

19.3 Food and Nutrition Board (FNB) is the technical wing of the Department in the
matter of implementation of VNP. Most of the scnemes, run under FNB, the Committees
notes with concern are not performing satisfactorily Targets fixed, both physical and
financial are not being uchieved. For example, the schemes for Fortification of Milk with
Vitamin ‘A’ is being implemented by only 54 dairies in the entire country. Fortification of
salt with Iron, as accepted by the Secretary, has been a non-starter due to some technical
problem. Important activities like Research and Development and quality control also do
not appear to have received due attention Progress of Mass Media Communication, which is
meant for creating awareness about nutrition, an important component of NNP, is also
tardy. Last but not the least the production of nutritious foods also appears to have fallen
upto rough weather and it has been decided not to sanction any grant on account of this in
future.

19.4 The Committee observes that a plethora of small schemes are being run in the field
of nutrition and food and the allocations made to them indicate that these are being run just
for the sake of running them. The Committee feels that it is better to have fewer schemes
and run them effectively and’efficiently, rather than having many of them and implementing
halfheartedly.

19.5 The Committee, therefore, feels that this is the high time that a review and
evaluation of all the schemes relating to food and nutrition should be done and important
and useful schemes should be strengthened accordingly. The Committee feels, it would be
desirable to restructure the scheme and arrange for the distribution of Vitamin ‘A’ and Iron
directly through ICDS.

20. The Committee is happy to know that the Department has already taken a lot of
interest and initiative for involving Panchayats and Nagar Palikas in the implementation and
monitoring of its programmes. The Department has also participated in organising awareness
generation and training programmes for elected members of the Panchayats; started Balvikas
Mahila Samitis for monitorifg all children and women related programmes at village, block
and district levels; and requested State Governments to form such Samitis. The Committee,
however, feels that the Department should take all necessary steps to seek more and more
participation and cooperation of the local bodies in implementing, monitoring, etc. of
various programmes meant for rural and semi-urban women and children.


21. It has been reported that ‘Sathin’ schemes has run into some difficulty because of
non-cooperation of Panchayats and a decision of the State Government of Rajasthan to
make them redundant. The Committee desires that the Department should take up the
matter with the concerned State to see that their services are utilised suitably.

PREFACE
          I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource
Development, having been authorised by the Committee, do hereby present on its behalf Two Hundred
Tenth Report of the Committee on 'Implementation of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA), Mid-Day Meal
(MDM) Scheme and Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) Scheme in Union Territories'.
2.       Over the years the implementation aspects of three major social schemes i.e. SSA, MDM and
ICDS have invariably been engaging the attention of the Committee during the examination of Demands
for Grants of various Ministries / Departments. The background of this study can actually be traced back
to the 4
th of October, 2004 when the Committee heard the Secretaries of the Department of School
Education and Literacy and Department of Women and Child Development in respect of different
Centrally sponsored schemes being operated by those departments in the country. Based on their
evidence, the Committee identified SSA, MDM and ICDS for detailed examination. Subsequently, the
study was focused to North-Eastern States and Jammu & Kashmir. The Committee has already presented
a report (193rd Report) on the implementation of these three schemes in North-Eastern States and Jammu
& Kashmir.
3.       In its meeting held on the 29 th November 2007, the Committee decided to continue its study on
these schemes with special focus on Union Territories.   The Committee undertook on the spot visits to
Union Territories of Puducherry, Lakshawdeep, Daman & Diu and Dadra & Nagar Haveli in two phases
in January and February, 2008 respectively. The Union Territory of Andaman & Nicobar Islands was a
part of the itinerary in the first phase of the Committee’s visit but was cancelled in view of the inability
expressed by the UT Administration due to some logistic problems. The Committee then heard the
representatives of the UT Administration of Andaman & Nicobar Islands along with the representatives
of Chandigarh and Delhi in the later half of May, 2008. 
4.       The Committee gained useful insights on the problems of implementation of the said schemes
during the on the spot study visits to Puducherry, Lakshawdeep, Daman & Diu and Dadra & Nagar
Haveli. The Committee would have liked to better appraise the implementation status through on-the-
spot visits of Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh and Delhi but for the paucity of time, their
representatives were called at Delhi for holding a discussion on these schemes.
5.       The Committee would like to express its gratitude to the Officers of the Department of School
Education and Literacy and the Ministry of Women and Child Development, Government of India as
well as to the Officers of Departments of Education and Social Welfare of Puducherry, Lakshadweep,
Andaman & Nicobar Islands, Daman & Diu, Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Chandigarh and Delhi for their
cooperation in furnishing the required material and information in connection with the examination of
these subjects and also making arrangements for the visit of the Committee.

___________________________________________________________________________REPORT
 
I.       INTRODUCTION
 
1.1     A brief introduction of the schemes considered by the Committee i.e. Sarva Siksha Abhiyan, Mid
Day Meal Scheme and Integrated Child Development Services Scheme followed by the status of their
implementation in the Union Territories is given below.
 
II.      SARVA SHIKSHA ABHIYAN (SSA)
 
BRIEF ON SSA
 
2.1     Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) is a national flagship programme of Government of India for
achieving the goal of Universalisation of Elementary Education (UEE) through a time bound approach,
as mandated by 86
th amendment to the Constitution of India making Free and Compulsory Education to
the Children of 6-14 age group, a Fundamental Right.
 
2.2     Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) was launched in 2001-02 to provide useful and relevant education
for all children in 6 to 14 age group in partnership with States and local bodies by the year 2010. SSA
cover seeks to ensure access, retention and quality improvement in elementary education. The
Programme also aims to bridge social, regional and gender gaps, with the active participation of the
community in the management of schools. The assistance under the SSA was in the sharing ratio of
85:15 between the Union and the States during the IX Plan and it was 75:25 during the X Plan. During
the XIth Plan, this ratio is being proposed to be brought down to 50:50 sharing between the Central
Government and State Government but in a phased manner i.e., funding pattern has been proposed as
65:35 for the first two years of the Plan period, 60:40 for the third year, 55:45 for the fourth year and
50:50 in the fifth year.
 
2.3     The Programme covers all the districts of the country and addresses the needs of 19.4 crore
children in 12.3 lakh habitations. The Programme seeks to open new schools in those habitations which
do not have schooling facilities and strengthen existing school infrastructure through provision of
additional class rooms, toilets, drinking water, maintenance grant and school improvement grants.
Existing schools with inadequate teacher strength are provided with additional teachers, while the
capacity of existing teachers is being strengthened by extensive training, grants for developing teaching-
learning materials and strengthening of the academic support structure at the cluster, block and district
level. SSA seeks to provide quality elementary education including life skills. SSA has a special focus on
girl education and children with special needs. SSA also seeks to provide computer education to bridge

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/210th%20Report.htm[01-07-2016 15:54:01]
the digital divide. The approach is community-owned and even the village education plans are prepared
locally in consultation with the Panchayati Raj Institutions.
 
IMPLEMENTATION OF SSA IN PUDUCHERRY
 
2.4     The Union Territory of Puducherry as per Census 2001 has a total population of 9,74,345 (486961
males and 487384 females). It comprises of four districts viz. Puducherry, Karaikal, Mahe and Yanam;
with six blocks and twenty five clusters.
 
2.5     The Committee undertook a study visit of Puducherry from the 20
th to the 22nd January, 2008 for
having first-hand experience about the implementation of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan there. The Committee
visited several schools in Puducherry. Some of the schools visited by the Committee include the Govt.
Middle School, Lawspet; Govt. Primary School, Sanarapet, Govt. Primary School, Thattanchavady; and
Kannagi Govt. Girls Hr. Sec. School, Vilianur.   It also interacted with the UT Administration officials,
teachers, students and community leaders to ascertain the practical difficulties being faced in the
implementation of the Programme.
 
2.6     The Committee was informed that the Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) at primary level decreased to
101% during 2006-07 which was 107.02% in 2005-06. However, there has been an improvement in GER
at upper primary level which was 99.7% in 2006-07 in comparison to 97.37% in 2005-06. The number of
out of school children had increased from 1724 children during 2005-06 to 2673 children during 2006-
07. Also, the drop out rate at primary level increased from 4.35% during 2005-06 to 4.43% during 2006-
07. The Committee finds these developments worrisome and it recommends to the Department and
the UT Administration to take corrective measures urgently.
 
2.7     Committee’s attention was drawn by the unsatisfactory level of education indicators specially in
respect of the district of Yanam. The Committee noted that Yanam had a very high drop-out rate of
17.33%. The district also suffered from a low GER of 80.2% at primary level. In Committee’s opinion,
such a high level of drop-out rate against quite a low GER called for corrective measures without any
delay. The Committee, accordingly, recommends to the UT Administration to take sincere steps to
improve the situation in Yanam. There was an urgent need to identify specific problem areas in
relation to Yanam followed by appropriate action.
 
2.8     The Committee noted that Puducherry is one of the few States/UTs which has failed to fully
realize the benefit of Alternative Schooling mode under SSA. In fact, the Committee has pointed out this
fact in its 201
st Report wherein it had observed that against a target of bringing 1724 children in
Alternative & Innovative Education (AIE) fold, only 94 children (5.45% of the target fixed) could
actually be covered till 31 st March, 2007. Also, during 2007-08, against the physical target of 2673
children under EGS/AIE scheme, the achievement level at the time of Committee's visit in January 2008
was nil. The Committee is unhappy over the lackadaisical approach of the UT Administration,
particularly when the drop-out rate and Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) are becoming adverse. The
Committee hopes that the UT Administration will take necessary steps to ensure that all the
components under SSA are optimally implemented so as to ensure maximum coverage of children
in the UT thereunder.
 

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/210th%20Report.htm[01-07-2016 15:54:01]
2.9     An outlay of Rs. 21.61 lakhs was provided for 2701 interventions for Children with Special Needs
(CWSN) during 2007-08. The Committee learnt that the UT Administration has completed identification
of CWSN. The Committee was informed that besides other initiatives like providing aids & appliances
and giving financial assistance, home based care and teaching were being given to 92 mentally retarded
students. The Committee appreciates such steps being taken for CWSN, especially mentally
retarded students. However, the Committee failed to meet any teacher/volunteer given specialized
training for taking care of the educational needs of such children during its study visit. The
Committee hopes that the UT Administration must have organised specialized training
programmes for teachers of CWSN.
 
2.10   The Committee notes that against a physical target of 2701 CWSN to be covered under the
Scheme of Integrated Education for Disabled during 2007-08, only 948 CWSN could be covered till
the 9
th January, 2008. Committee’s attention has been drawn by the physical targets remaining
under-achieved under this vital component during the previous three years also. The Committee
finds this unacceptable and recommends that the UT Administration should make all efforts for
inclusion of all the identified CWSN and not repeat the past performance of under-achieving the
physical targets. Necessary funds for the purpose may be provided.
 
2.11   The Committee was informed by the UT Administration that all the schools were provided with
good infrastructure facilities, especially building and furniture under SSA. However, the Committee
noted that progress under civil works has been dismal, especially in respect of construction of school
buildings and additional class-rooms. The following table illustrates the position:-
 
Year School buildings Additional class rooms
Target Achievement Target Achievement
2004-05 25 Nil 91 Nil
2005-06 13 Nil 238 166
2006-07 13 Nil 72 5
 
2.12   The Committee finds that this dismal trend has continued in 2007-08 also with only four school
buildings being completed against a target of ten school buildings. The Committee is at a loss to
comprehend the factors responsible for such an approach of the UT Administration. In fact, due to
such a tardy progress in civil works, the Project Approval Board did not agree to any fresh civil
works for the UT of Puducherry for the year 2007-08. The Committee also finds that pace of other
civil works like construction of toilets, drinking water facilities, Block Resource Centres (BRCs)
and Cluster Resource Centres (CRCs) has also been discouraging. The Committee is all the more
disturbed by the fact that inspite of funds being duly allocated all these years, UT Administration
has simply failed to take benefit of the same. The Committee would like both the Department and
the UT Administration to take corrective measures so as to ensure removal of all the problem
areas. Obviously, it is high time to focus on the quality of education under SSA. The civil works
cannot be allowed to linger on indefinitely simply because good infrastructure is a pre-condition
for retention of students and quality education.
 
2.13   The Committee was given to understand that all the teachers have been given training for a period
of 8-10 days per year mainly on curriculum enrichment, ICT and other innovative practices. This fact, is

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/210th%20Report.htm[01-07-2016 15:54:01]
however, not borne out by the dismal utilisation level under the component of Teachers Training under
SSA. The Committee notes that against a financial target of Rs.79.78 lakhs during 2004-05, the
actual expenditure was a mere Rs.8.85 lakhs; in 2005-06 only Rs.15.18 lakhs were spent against an
allocation of Rs.75.87 lakhs and in 2006-07 against an allocation of Rs.73.52 lakhs, only Rs.9.97
lakhs could be spent. The situation continues to be discouraging as against an allocation of
Rs.67.98 lakhs during 2007-08 only Rs.4.57 lakhs could be spent as on 09.01.2008. The Committee
is perturbed to note that the position seems to have deteriorated further during the last two years
as against a target of 5061 and 4807 teachers to be trained in 2006-07 and 2007-08 respectively,
only 1467 and 520 (upto 9th Jan, 2008) could be trained. The Committee strongly feels that neglect
of teachers' training may have adversely affected the quality of education in the UT of Puducherry.
The Committee desires to underline the fact that education without quality will not serve any
purpose. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the UT Administration should take
corrective measures so that the targets fixed under Teachers' Training are fully achieved.
 
2.14   Committee’s attention has been drawn by the findings of survey of implementation of SSA in
Puducherry conducted by the designated Monitoring Institute, i.e. Puducherry University. The
Committee notes that this study was conducted in 36 schools out of 382 schools covered under SSA
Programme in Puducherry during the period from 1
st April to 30 th September, 2007. 35 schools were
Govt. Schools and only one school run with Govt. Aid. While overall performance level of SSA
Programme in the schools visited by the monitoring team was found to be very encouraging, a number of
areas requiring improvement have been pointed out in the Study Report. Some major shortcomings are
indicated below:-
 
-                     Civil works are very weak in few schools, many primary schools need new class rooms.
-                     Education Inspector needs to be empowered to monitor frequently the implementation of SSA
Programme.
-                     Training component of teachers not very satisfactory. Need for having more training
programmes emphasised by the teachers themselves.
-                     Lack of awareness about the aims and objectives of SSA noticed in teachers.
-                     Twice a year Refresher Training Programme required for the school Headmaster and School
Co-ordinator.
-                     No visits to schools so far by the CRC and BRC Co-ordinators.
-                     VECs not being involved in the running of schools as envisaged under SSA.
-                     Cash books in schools not being maintained properly and records also not being updated.
-                     Funds allocated to the schools as maintenance/ school grants were not being used in time. In
many schools, account balance was too high.  Proper guidelines need to be issued in this regard.
-                     VEC/SSA meetings being not attended by the Headmasters, instead representatives being sent
by them, leading to communication gap.
-                     Accounts about TLM amount not being submitted by the Teachers.
 
2.15   The Committee observes that although the survey conducted by the Puducherry University is
only a sample study, it gives a fair idea about the practical problem areas evident at the ground
level.  The Committee hopes that required follow-up action must have been taken by the concerned
authorities both at the UT and Central level by now. The Committee would like to be apprised
about the same. The aforesaid assessment pertained to the first half of the year 2007-08. The

REPORT
file:///D/Committee%20on%20HRD/210th%20Report.htm[01-07-2016 15:54:01]
Committee hopes that the report about the second half of the year 2007-08 must have been
received by now. Committee’s apprehensions have arisen because as per the details available with
the Committee, similar assessment for the second half of the year 2006-07 seems to have not been
conducted. The Committee can only emphasise that the very purpose of monitoring of SSA
programme by independent institutions would be defeated if any missing links/ gaps are there.
 
IMPLEMENTATION OF SSA IN LAKSHADWEEP
 
2.16   The Union Territory of Lakshadweep comprises of 27 islands in the Arabian Sea between 8 o and
12o -30' north latitude and between 71 st and 74 th east longitude at a distance ranging from 200 kms to
400 kms from mainland. Of the 27 islands, only ten islands are inhabited while the other islands are
small and exist as satellites of the inhabited islands. The total population of Lakshadweep is around
60,650. Lakshadweep is the 4 th densely populated area after Delhi, Chandigarh and Puducherry. Area-
wise, Andrott is the largest island with a population of 10727 while Bangaram is the smallest of them all
with a population of only 65.   
 
2.17   The Committee visited the Union Territory between the 4 th to 6th February, 2008. The Committee
had the opportunity to visit some schools in the two main islands in Lakshadweep, namely Kavaratti
(which happens to be the second largest inhabited island) and Agatti (the fifth largest inhabited island). 
 
2.18   The Lakshadweep Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan State Mission Authority was established in 2002 to
fulfill the aim of Universalisation of Elementary Education. A separate Management system has been set
up to look after the implementation of SSA in the Directorate of Education in January, 2007.
 
Allocations under SSA
 
2.19   The Committee was informed that a total of Rs.288.32 lakhs has been allocated to the SSA
Mission since its inception in 2002-03. Of this allocation, the expenditure incurred was Rs.175.15 lakhs
till January, 2008. Year-wise details of the funds received and the expenditure incurred since 2002-03 on
